title: When AI Chooses for Consumers: Machine Legibility and the Representation Advantage
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Management and Columbia University

detail.title: When AI Chooses for Consumers: Machine Legibility and the Representation Advantage
detail.abstract: When consumers delegate choice to AI, each platform record must inform both the shopper and the agent. We develop machine legibility, a record-level construct capturing whether task-relevant information appears in category-appropriate fields. An organizing model shows how exposing or completing these fields creates a representation advantage. We validate the construct with 33.37 million real marketplace actions and test its consequences in 140,060 controlled choices across four AI families. Three findings emerge. First, labeled information shifts AI toward alternatives whose records contain 11.7 percentage points more relevant fields; randomized tests reproduce this effect across four attributes with content fixed. Second, audited placement of a seller-supplied brand raises target selection by 15.1 points, whereas an irrelevant field does not. Third, representation changes brands and prices but moves agreement with observed purchases by 0.6 points. Record design is a platform-controlled basis of competition even when products and seller claims remain unchanged.

title: Branding the Consumer Spread Mind
affiliations: and IULM University

detail.title: Branding the Consumer Spread Mind

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper takes advantage of a new theory of mind (the Spread Mind) that challenges the axioms of the traditional branding ontology of the consumer as a rational agent. The new theory of mind equates consumers with non-cognitive objects embedded in a network of causal relationships and shifts the focus of branding from the consumer's subjective mind to a collective level of networked intelligence. This conceptual shift endorses a new ontology that views branding-and by extension marketing-as independent of other mentalistic disciplines and supports an alternative perspective in terms of viewing consumers' minds as a spread network of social interactions as the actual source of value and as focus of marketing actions. We posit a set of propositions to link the Spread Mind theory to branding and find support for this in the recent developments in multiple streams of literature that converge to form a coherent and evolved framework for understanding brands in today's globalized sociocultural environment.

title: How Artificial Intelligence Reconfigures Strategic Alignment in B2B Partnerships: A RAMESES-Informed Realist Synthesis of Context-Mechanism-Outcome Configurations
affiliations: and Islamic Azad University (IAU) - Islamic Azad University (IAU)

detail.title: How Artificial Intelligence Reconfigures Strategic Alignment in B2B Partnerships: A RAMESES-Informed Realist Synthesis of Context-Mechanism-Outcome Configurations
detail.abstract: in some partnerships and erode it in others. This RAMESES-informed realist synthesis of 27 peer-reviewed empirical studies (2018-June 2025) asks how, for whom, under what conditions, and through which mechanisms AI reconfigures long-term inter-organizational alignment. Dual screening and coding, MMAT appraisal, CERQual grading, explicit CMOC consolidation rules, rival/negative cases, and multiple sensitivity analyses support a mid-range program theory with three interdependent pathways-Technology-Operational Enablement, Relational-Social Calibration, and Governance-Structural Institutionalization-conditioned by six moderators and bounded by failure modes such as power-asymmetry amplification, verification-bottleneck transfer, and black-box vendor lock-in. Canonical trust bases are treated as differentially activated under AI mediation rather than as a new taxonomy. Corpus-grounded mechanisms are separated from theory-extended design scaffolds. The result is a configurational account of AI-B2B alignment with transparent methods and actionable governance implications for industrial marketing and alliance management.

title: Dynamic Cross-Level Mechanisms of Generative AI Adoption: Motivations, Affordances, and Ethical Reasoning among Designers and Non-Designers
affiliations: National Taiwan University, EMLYON Business School, , Virginia Tech - Pamplin College of Business and Shih Chien University

detail.title: Dynamic Cross-Level Mechanisms of Generative AI Adoption: Motivations, Affordances, and Ethical Reasoning among Designers and Non-Designers
detail.abstract: GAI tools such as ChatGPT, Canva, Runway, and Midjourney are reshaping creative work by enabling collaborative human-AI practices that extend well beyond automation. Yet how diverse users adopt, adapt, and sustain engagement with GAI remains underexplored. Using a trajectory perspective, we propose a cross-level framework explaining how designers and non-designers engage with GAI across three contextual modes: acceptance, continued use, and loyal use. The framework integrates selfdetermination theory to account for individual motivations, affordance theory to capture system capabilities, and a duty-virtue-consequentialist lens to explain ethical reasoning. We show how these dynamics co-evolve as users move across contexts. Using a sequential mixed-methods approach (30 interviews, 15,000 online posts, and a survey of 507 participants), we find non-designers initially foreground intrinsic curiosity and emotional-relational affordances. As their use shifts toward productivity, cognitive affordances and extrinsic motivations become more salient, while emotional and relational affordances recede but remain available. Designers, by contrast, emphasize competence driven cognitive affordances and duty-consequentialist ethics in contexts of high professional accountability. As their creative autonomy expands, they increasingly draw on emotional and relational affordances, autonomy needs, and virtue-oriented reflection. Across both groups, GAI engagement reflects shifting contextual priorities rather than linear progression, with multiple affordances activated in parallel. A virtue-ethics paradox also emerges: heightened virtue-based reflection can constrain designers’ long-term loyalty by intensifying concerns about authenticity and professional identity. We advance post-adoption, SDT, and affordance theories by demonstrating that GAI engagement is dynamic, multi-level, and feedback-driven, and it provides guidance for designing adaptive, ethically grounded human–AI collaboration systems.

title: A Signal-Based Scoring Model for Customer Advocacy Readiness in B2B SaaS

detail.title: A Signal-Based Scoring Model for Customer Advocacy Readiness in B2B SaaS
detail.abstract:
Customer marketing and advocacy professionals in B2B SaaS organizations lack structured data driven approaches to identify and engage customers for advocacy and marketing needs. Practitioners often rely on isolated metrics and data like the Net Promoter Score (NPS) survey results or informal discussions and judgments from revenue teams in an ad-hoc manner.
This paper proposes a single and structured signal based scoring model integrating distinct customer signals including survey based customer feedback, production adoption and usage information, renewal status, potential for expansion (and cross-sell, up-sell), history of customer’s advocacy participation, interesting product use cases, customer’s professional journey and involvement in the industry, and feedback from internal teams into a blended scoring system to assess advocacy readiness at both account and individual contact level.
This framework is designed to be scalable, replicable, adaptable across different B2B organizations of varying sizes and business models.
This paper aims to contribute to the marketing function and provides a practical alternative to the current unstructured advocacy selection processes. It also offers a foundation for future empirical validation.

title: To go Public or Private: Handling Consumer Complaints from a Dynamic Triadic Perspective
affiliations: National Taiwan University, EMLYON Business School, , Virginia Tech - Pamplin College of Business and Shih Chien University

detail.title: To go Public or Private: Handling Consumer Complaints from a Dynamic Triadic Perspective

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

detail.abstract: When firms respond to social media complaints with “Please DM us,” why do some consumers comply while others publicly resist? We examine this question by studying how complaints evolve as online audiences become involved. Using Twitter field data, experiments, and interviews, we identify three stages of emotional escalation and show that effective recovery depends on matching firm responses to these stages. Our findings reveal two key insights. First, appreciation is more strongly associated with favorable public outcomes than apology, particularly as complaints intensify. Second, although explanations remain essential, compensation presents a paradox: at high emotional intensity, it improves public-resolution evaluations, whereas field and interview evidence suggests that private compensation offers may be resisted as consumers prioritize public accountability over private gain. We explain this tension as a strategic trade-off between public validation and private problem-solving. For managers, we offer a stage-based framework clarifying when to invite private contact, when to act proactively, and when public acknowledgment is necessary.

title: From Cognition to Action: The Effect of Thought Self- Leadership Strategies and Self-Monitoring on Adaptive  Selling Behavior

detail.title: From Cognition to Action: The Effect of Thought Self- Leadership Strategies and Self-Monitoring on Adaptive  Selling Behavior
detail.abstract: Purpose-This study aims to investigate salespersons' self-monitoring and its effect on adaptive selling behavior. As salespeople are constantly facing different customers with various needs and want and engaging in a different sales situation, salespeople must deploy their inner capabilities in practicing adaptive selling behavior during and across sales interactions. This study also investigates the impact of salesperson's intrapersonal leadershipwhere leadership stems from the individuals with the purpose to influence oneself. Design/methodology/approach-Authors draw on the social cognitive theory of self-regulation to develop our model and examine the relationship between self-monitoring, thought self-leadership and adaptive selling behavior. We empirically test the model using data from 335 pharmaceutical salespeople working across several countries in Asia. Findings-The results support the role of self-monitoring and thought self-leadership as antecedents to adaptive selling. Further, the results suggest that self-monitoring positively moderates the relationship between thought self-leadership and adaptive selling behavior. In light of these results, we explore implications and limitations and conclude by suggesting directions for further research. Research limitations/implications-The sampling method used was convenience sampling, which may limit the theoretical generalization of our results across all emerging markets. Moreover, this study examines the direct impact of self-management mechanism on adaptive selling behavior and the way it interacts with salesperson's thought self-leadership to strengthen adaptive selling behavior. However, the research model does not include organization-level drivers. Originality/value-This study makes an important and original contribution to sales literature by demonstrating the direct and interaction effects of self-monitoring mechanism on a critical component of a business to business sales process, adaptive selling behavior. Results from this study highlight the critical importance of cognitive processes that drives positive selling behavior.

title:
Beyond the Mainstream Domain 
A Page-Level Audit of Editorial, Corporate, and Commercial Content in AI Citation Sources in Indonesia
affiliations: Universitas Prasetiya Mulya

detail.title:
Beyond the Mainstream Domain 
A Page-Level Audit of Editorial, Corporate, and Commercial Content in AI Citation Sources in Indonesia

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was self-funded by the author. The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: Generative search systems increasingly answer questions by synthesizing selected web sources, making citation composition consequential for publishers, firms, and users. Yet source audits commonly classify citations at the domain level, potentially conflating independent journalism with press-release-derived, native, sponsored, or commerce-oriented pages hosted by the same publisher. This study introduces the Host-Provenance Citation Framework, which separates institutional host identity from page-level content provenance, and applies it to four anonymized AI citation audits conducted in Indonesia in 2026. The dataset contains 1,714 captured citation occurrences from 473 responses and 36 audit-specific prompts across Google AI Mode, Gemini, and ChatGPT, representing 732 canonical unique pages on 315 domains. URLs were canonicalized, within-response duplicates were flagged, and a purposively constructed 51-URL blind second-coder sample was used to validate the host taxonomy. Mainstream/news domains accounted for 54 of 1,714 captured citation occurrences (3.15%) and 54 of 1,664 after within-response deduplication (3.25%). Among mainstream occurrences, 42 (77.78%) remained editorial or provenance-unclear, nine (16.67%) were commerce or affiliate-oriented, two (3.70%) were press-release-derived, and one (1.85%) appeared in a native or sponsored section. The pattern was stable at the page level: seven of 31 unique mainstream pages (22.58%) were release-derived, native-section, or commerce-oriented, compared with 12 of 54 occurrence-weighted citations (22.22%). Within the purposive validation sample, primary-category agreement was 94.12% (Cohen's kappa = 0.901), while binary mainstream classification achieved 100% agreement (kappa = 1.00). Mainstream publishers were therefore present but not dominant, and host identity alone did not establish independent editorial provenance. The study contributes a reproducible framework while remaining bounded: the counts describe captured citation composition, not model trust, page usefulness, or the causal effectiveness of mainstream publication. For the emerging AI Visibility Optimization research agenda, the evidence supports examining both where information appears and how clearly a citable page's provenance can be interpreted.

title: Harnessing the Power Within: The Consequences of Salesperson Moral Identity and the Moderating Role of Internal Competitive Climate
affiliations: and Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge - E.J. Ourso College of Business Administration

detail.title: Harnessing the Power Within: The Consequences of Salesperson Moral Identity and the Moderating Role of Internal Competitive Climate
detail.abstract: The purpose of this research is to examine the notion of salesperson moral identity as a prosocial individual trait and its associated effects on customer and coworker relationships. In addition, this study examines the underlying processes in which these effects occur as well as the moderating role of internal competitive climate. Our empirical investigation of business-to-business (B2B) sales professionals reveals that moral identity has both direct and indirect effects on a salesperson's customer and team-directed outcomes. Specifically, our results demonstrate that salesperson moral identity positively affects both salesperson-customer identification and organizational identification, which, in turn, impact customer service provision and teamwork. Our findings also indicate that internal competitive climate exacerbates the positive effects of salesperson moral identity on customer service provision and teamwork.

title: How Vulnerable Are Consumer Research Surveys to AI Agents? Validating an Instrument-Review Framework and Auditing Recent JCR Open Materials
affiliations: University of California Los Angeles, , Olin Business School, Washington University in St. Louis and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management

detail.title: How Vulnerable Are Consumer Research Surveys to AI Agents? Validating an Instrument-Review Framework and Auditing Recent JCR Open Materials

declarations.ethicsApproval: This research has been certified as exempt from UCLA's IRB review per 45 CFR 46.104 category 3
declarations.funderStatement: The authors gratefully acknowledge support from the Morrison Center for Marketing and Data Analytics.

detail.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence have produced agents that can complete online surveys while passing the checks consumer researchers commonly rely on, yet data-quality practice still treats the respondent, rather than the instrument, as the unit of evaluation. We introduce Survey-Shield, an open-source instrument-review tool that scores surveys against a rubric of eight bot-resistance categories, and validate the rubric directly. A factorial experiment manipulates the presence of each category across 256 survey versions and exposes each version to AI agents built from three frontier language models. In an interim sample from a planned 3,840 bot runs, categories relying on interface-level or mechanical signals (Metadata and CAPTCHA, Mouse and Keyboard Input) are evaded least often, while categories relying on a language model's reasoning (Logic, Refusal Probes, Context Awareness) are evaded substantially more often, and the ordering varies by model. We derive empirically grounded rubric weights from these rates and apply them to 252 instruments from 37 JCR articles with deposited Qualtrics files, of 312 indexed between 2021 and 2026. These instruments were designed against an earlier threat, human inattention rather than automated agents, so the audit speaks to the field's current exposure rather than to past research quality: the modal instrument offers little resistance to contemporary AI agents, and the categories most often missing are not the categories most responsible for stopping them. We report interim results while data collection continues and close with recommendations for researchers, journals, and platforms.

title: The Impact of Business-Tobusiness Salespeople's Social Media Use on Value Co-Creation and Cross/Up-Selling: The Role of Social Capital
affiliations: , Texas State University, Texas State University and IESEG School of Management

detail.title: The Impact of Business-Tobusiness Salespeople's Social Media Use on Value Co-Creation and Cross/Up-Selling: The Role of Social Capital
detail.abstract: Purpose-This study aims to develop and test a process model of the effect of social media use by business-to-business (B2B) salespeople on their value cocreation and cross/upselling performance. Adopting a research acquisition perspective, the authors claim that salesperson's social media use is critical for generating social capitalan operant resource characterized by superior market knowledge, reputation and networkingwhich, in turn, directly and synergistically enhances value cocreation and cross/upselling outcomes. Design/methodology/approach-A model is developed based on extant sales research on salesperson's social media use and social capital theory. Data from B2B salespeople is analyzed using structural equation modeling to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings-The results demonstrate that salespeople's social media use enhances their social capital with support for direct effects on market knowledge and reputation, and indirect effect on networking. The results also show that the three aspects of social capital drive value cocreation, which enhances cross/upselling performance. Post hoc analysis shows the indirect effects of salesperson's social media use as well as the interconnected effects of the aspects of social capital on value cocreation. Practical implications-The study indicates that salespeople should be encouraged to use social media as a means for enhancing market knowledge and reputation, which can then be leveraged to build networking skills. Providing training to salespeople and coaching them on how to build their social capital is essential if organizations need to capitalize on novel ways to improve the value cocreation performance of their sales teams. Originality/value-This study demonstrates how salespeople's social media use can enhance their social capital, which, in turn, is critical for value cocreation and cross/upselling performance. The proposed framework opens opportunities for future studies to examine the role of salesperson social capital and value cocreation in B2B exchanges.

title: Decision Drift: A Sequential Architecture for Product-Market Decisions

detail.title: Decision Drift: A Sequential Architecture for Product-Market Decisions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests, personal relationships, or other conflicts of interest that could have influenced the work presented in this manuscript. The anonymised advisory cases are drawn from the author's professional advisory practice and are presented solely for conceptual illustration without identifying clients or confidential information.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript presents a conceptual framework supported by anonymised advisory cases and analyses of publicly documented business cases. It does not involve human participants, patient data, surveys, interviews, or experiments requiring institutional ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was independently conceived, developed, and completed by the author.

detail.abstract:
Decision drift operates across organisational domains. This paper examines its manifestation in product-market decisions — the sequence of moves a company makes to match an asset to a market and convert that match into revenue.

Product-market decisions are challenging not because the analysis is wrong but because they bear multi-layered simultaneous assumptions — about where the product is in its lifecycle, what resources are required versus available, what actually moves the needle, and what constitutes critical mass for the specific buyer in the specific market. When these assumptions are inherited rather than examined, the effort goes in a coherent direction that turns out to be the wrong one.

This paper introduces the Decision Drift Check (DDC), a practitioner diagnostic for product-market decisions across entry, product-market fit, and growth. DDC classifies the decision across two dimensions — the problem being solved and the asset being used to solve it — producing four categories: Prove, Promote, Pioneer, and Push. Each category has different minimum requirements for asset readiness and adoption friction, different market reality checks, and different context modifiers that determine what the one-step move actually requires.

DDC works in two passes. The forward pass maps the practitioner’s current position honestly across four dimensions: asset friction, adoption friction, demand validation, and competitive space. The stage reading emerges from the forward pass as a derived output, not an upfront assumption. The reverse pass identifies the single most constrained dimension and traces what moving it one step requires. The two most load-bearing dependencies emerge from this trace — not from a generic checklist but from the specific requirements of that one movement in that specific context.

The framework is applied across six cases spanning all four decision categories. Three cases are drawn from the author’s advisory practice, presented in anonymised form. Three cases — Jio, AWS, and the L’Oréal/Innovist transaction — apply DDC to publicly available information. One public transaction is examined from both sides of the table. One public case traces the same asset across three points in time, demonstrating DDC’s dynamic reclassification as markets mature.

DDC does not replace practitioner judgment. It makes judgment’s assumptions visible, so they can be examined rather than inherited.

title: When Poignant Stories Outweigh Cold Hard Facts: A Meta-Analysis of the Anecdotal Bias

detail.title: When Poignant Stories Outweigh Cold Hard Facts: A Meta-Analysis of the Anecdotal Bias
detail.abstract: The objective of this paper is to resolve mixed findings about which type of evidence is more persuasive-statistical or anecdotal information. In a meta-analysis of 61 papers exploring the persuasive impact of evidence type, we establish that, in situations where emotional engagement is high (e.g., an issue associated with a severe threat, involving a health issue, or affecting oneself), statistical evidence is less influential than anecdotal evidence. However, in situations where emotional engagement is relatively low (e.g., an issue associated with low threat severity, involving a non-health issue, or affecting others), statistical evidence is more persuasive than anecdotal evidence. We discuss the theoretical and practical implications of these findings, and how to improve persuasive messaging by considering the contextual effectiveness of both anecdotes and statistics.

title: Partisan Résumés: ESG Signaling over the Political Cycle
affiliations: McDonough School of Business, Mitchell E. Daniels, Jr School of Business, Purdue University and Harvard University - Business School (HBS)

detail.title: Partisan Résumés: ESG Signaling over the Political Cycle
detail.abstract: We examine how political ideology shapes labor market signals. Using proprietary data on résumé edits, we identify additions and deletions of ESG-related language in descriptions of past roles. We find that these revisions are shaped by both workers' political ideology and the broader political environment. Democrat-leaning workers are more likely than Republicanleaning workers to add ESG language to their résumés, with this partisan divide widening during the Biden administration. Vague, unspecific additions appear most strategic, as they are disproportionately reversed following the start of Trump's second term. Exploiting the staggered adoption of ESG commitments by large corporations during the Biden presidency, we find that workers who view these firms as potential employers increase their use of ESG language relative to other workers. These revisions are associated with tangible career benefits, including greater job mobility and higher promotion rates. They also distort labor market matching by helping less qualified workers obtain positions, and potentially impose hiring costs on employers.

title: Strategic AI Sourcing in Telecommunications Operations: A Governance-Oriented Framework for External, Vendor-Managed, Private, and Hybrid AI Models

detail.title: Strategic AI Sourcing in Telecommunications Operations: A Governance-Oriented Framework for External, Vendor-Managed, Private, and Hybrid AI Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a practice-informed conceptual framework and does not involve human participants, interviews, surveys, clinical data, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly relevant to telecommunications operations, including service assurance, customer operations, network-related workflows, operational knowledge support, anomaly detection, automation, and decision support. However, responsible AI adoption depends not only on technical capability, but also on how AI capabilities are sourced, governed, controlled, monitored, and sustained.
This paper develops a governance-oriented conceptual framework for AI sourcing in telecommunications operations. It addresses the decision gap that appears when organizations have access to public AI tools, vendor-managed enterprise AI platforms, private AI deployment options, and hybrid architectures, but lack a structured method for matching sourcing models to use-case risk, data sensitivity, operational criticality, capability maturity, auditability, vendor dependency, and strategic control.
The paper proposes the Telecommunications AI Sourcing Decision Framework (TASDF). The framework consists of nine decision dimensions: use-case criticality, data sensitivity and boundary, control and customization need, auditability and explainability, integration and observability, cost and scalability, capability maturity, vendor dependency with portability and reversibility, and regulatory and contractual accountability. The framework is designed to help organizations evaluate external/public AI, vendor-managed enterprise AI, internal/private AI, and hybrid AI models in a structured and proportional way.
The paper argues that no AI sourcing model is universally superior. External AI may support speed and low-cost experimentation for low-risk tasks. Vendor-managed enterprise AI may provide domain capability and faster implementation with contractual and technical controls. Internal/private AI may offer stronger control, customization, and data protection, but requires higher organizational maturity. Hybrid AI may balance speed and control, but only when data boundaries, architecture, monitoring, and accountability are clearly governed.
The paper's contribution is a practical decision framework that supports responsible AI sourcing in telecommunications and similar technology-driven environments. The paper does not claim empirical validation. Instead, it offers a structured conceptual model for sector discussion, internal assessment, future research, and more disciplined AI sourcing decisions.

title: Information Decay Need Not Yield a Transitive Completion of the Blackwell Order
affiliations: Reichman University

detail.title: Information Decay Need Not Yield a Transitive Completion of the Blackwell Order
detail.abstract: Blackwell's order is incomplete. We ask whether information decay can produce a complete and transitive extension of it. First, two positive doubly stochastic Markov kernels may converge to the same null-information matrix while their powers remain Blackwell incomparable at every finite horizon. Second, the comparison relation based on directed Markov crossing times is a complete extension on the domain of invertible primitive kernels but admits a strict three-cycle. Third, the analogous relation based on linear mixing with null information is also a complete extension but non-transitive. Thus, direct comparison under decay may remain incomplete, while the two natural decay-based completion rules studied here fail transitivity.

title: The Algorithmic Underwriting Deficit: Navigating Data Quality, Bias, and Auditability in Emerging Market AI-Driven Credit Systems

detail.title: The Algorithmic Underwriting Deficit: Navigating Data Quality, Bias, and Auditability in Emerging Market AI-Driven Credit Systems

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or non-profit sectors. The author conducted this study independently.

detail.abstract: In emerging economies across Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and Latin America, the informal sector represents between 61% and 90% of total economic activity (International Labour Organization [ILO], 2018). Characterized by cash-based transactions, irregular income velocity, and an absence of formalized regulatory documentation-such as tax records or centralized credit histories-the financial profiles of these populations remain profoundly marginalized within traditional credit bureaus. Consequently, emerging artificial intelligence (AI)-driven fintech platforms rely heavily on alternative, fragmented data footprints harvested across disparate sources, including mobile network operators, utility payment records, and microfinance ledgers (Björkegren & Grissen, 2019). This paper examines how the localized, non-unified, and highly volatile nature of this alternative data creates an "algorithmic underwriting deficit." We argue that the structural data quality disparities in these regions inherently undermine the core principles of Responsible AI, specifically impeding the mathematical validation of fairness, algorithmic robustness, system explainability, and corporate accountability in automated credit-scoring mechanisms (Barocas & Selbst, 2016; Raji et al., 2020). Finally, we propose a socio-technical governance framework designed to establish decentralized data assurance and risk auditing protocols tailored specifically to informal economic models.

title: Formalizing the Invisible Hand: Informational Efficiency in Production Trees
affiliations: King’s College London

detail.title: Formalizing the Invisible Hand: Informational Efficiency in Production Trees

declarations.declarationOfInterest: nothing to declare
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: The invisible hand has two canonical interpretations. Arrow and Debreu formalized the allocative one in the welfare theorems. The epistemic one of Hayek (1945) and Friedman and Friedman (1980), for whom Read's I, Pencil argued that the market coordinates a division of knowledge no single mind possesses, has been formalized only where the commodity space is fixed. There the price system is minimal, and uniquely so, in exchange (Mount and Reiter 1974; Jordan 1982) and with single-stage production (Tian 2006). But the Hayek-Friedman interpretation also concerns coordination across stages of production, and what happens as those stages multiply. We extend the informational-size framework to production-tree economies, where the final good emerges from a branching tree of stages, each operated by an agent knowing only his own technology. A participant's informational burden is set by his number of direct suppliers, hence invariant to the tree's depth and size; the price mechanism's message space has minimal dimension. No regular informational mechanism asks less of any participant (provided income is not redistributed). By contrast, any single mind that would determine the entire allocation must resolve a space as large as the tree, and growing with it. This model gives a more general and formal treatment of the epistemic invisible hand, in a setting where the production network can grow. The division of knowledge can deepen without limit; what each participant must know does not grow with it.

title:
Privacy-preserving Federated Graph Neural Networks for Collaborative Intrusion Detection 

A Framework Integrating Graph Neural Networks, Federated Learning, and Differential Privacy for Distributed Network Security
affiliations: Dharmsinh Desai University

detail.title:
Privacy-preserving Federated Graph Neural Networks for Collaborative Intrusion Detection 

A Framework Integrating Graph Neural Networks, Federated Learning, and Differential Privacy for Distributed Network Security
detail.abstract: The escalating scale and heterogeneity of modern network infrastructures have exposed the limitations of intrusion detection systems (IDS) that rely on centralized data collection, both in terms of scalability and data-privacy compliance. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as an effective paradigm for network intrusion detection because network traffic naturally maps onto graph structures in which hosts or flows form nodes and communications form edges [2], [3], [5]. Independently, federated learning (FL) has become the dominant approach for training machine learning models across organizationally or geographically distributed data owners without centralizing raw data [1], [7]. This paper proposes PP-FedGNN-IDS, a framework that unifies these two paradigms to enable multiple organizations to collaboratively train a shared graph-based intrusion detection model while keeping raw traffic graphs local to each participant. The framework combines an edge-feature-aware GraphSAGE-style local encoder with a federated averaging protocol, and layers two complementary privacy mechanisms on top of the aggregation process: client-level local differential privacy for gradient perturbation and cryptographic secure aggregation to prevent the central server from inspecting individual updates [8], [9], [10]. We formalize the threat model under honest-but-curious and Byzantine adversaries, describe the end-to-end architecture, and present an evaluation protocol grounded in widely used benchmark datasets (NSL-KDD, CICIDS2017, Bot-IoT, and ToN_IoT) together with a structured comparison against recent federated graph-learning intrusion detection systems reported in the literature [15], [19], [20], [21], [23]. The analysis indicates that combining structural graph representations with federated privacy mechanisms can preserve detection accuracy that approaches centralized GNN baselines while providing formal privacy guarantees and resistance to gradient-leakage and poisoning attacks. We conclude by outlining open challenges around non-independent-and-identically-distributed (non-IID) graph partitions, communication overhead, and the privacy-utility trade-off that remain central to deploying federated graph learning for cybersecurity at scale.

title: The Quantum-AI Invention Stack: Patent Strategy, Inventorship, and Disclosure Timing as AI Accelerates Quantum R&D

detail.title: The Quantum-AI Invention Stack: Patent Strategy, Inventorship, and Disclosure Timing as AI Accelerates Quantum R&D
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence and quantum computing are converging into a layered research environment, referred to herein as a quantum-AI invention stack, in which technical advances emerge from interactions among human researchers, AI systems, quantum hardware, calibration and errorcorrection workflows, compilers, and simulation tools. This essay argues that the convergence tests patent law without displacing it. Its central claim is that acceleration converts documentation and disclosure timing from administrative questions into substantive legal ones: quantum-AI research teams should record conception, selection, validation, and ownership decisions while the research is still moving, and should treat the choice of what to disclose, when, and through which channel as an innovation-governance problem with a single owner and a single clock. Two further claims frame that argument. AI-assisted quantum inventions should remain patentable where natural persons make the legally required inventive contribution, and the patent system's disclosure bargain should be preserved, including in security-sensitive fields such as quantum cryptanalysis. The essay closes with five policy principles for patent practice and innovation governance in the quantum-AI era, and with concrete steps for implementing them.

title: The Effects of Blockchain-based Track and Trace on Consumer Returns
affiliations: , University of Iowa - Department of Business Analytics, Lehigh University - College of Business, China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) and China Europe International Business School (CEIBS)

detail.title: The Effects of Blockchain-based Track and Trace on Consumer Returns
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Annual U.S. merchandise returns approach $850 billion, a cost driven by information asymmetry that persists after delivery. Blockchain-based track and trace (BCT) makes supply-chain information verifiable, yet its business value is framed almost entirely around upstream operational benefits. The effect of BCT on post-purchase consumer behavior, particularly the costly decision to return a product, remains empirically untested. We examine whether BCT reduces consumer product returns, identify the product categories in which this effect emerges, and uncover the informational mechanism that drives it. Methodology/results: Exploiting the partial adoption of BCT across products at a leading global online retailer, we apply a quasi-experimental design with matched controls across product categories. BCT reduces product return rates by 2.64 percentage points, a roughly 60% reduction from the baseline mean. The effect is concentrated in experience goods (where consumers verify quality through use) and is null for credence goods (where quality remains unobservable after use), a pattern consistent with an information-based mechanism. Consistent with this mechanism, BCT improves consumers' perceived information reliability. We further find suggestive evidence of a cognitive pathway: using large language models validated against human annotators, we show that BCT shifts consumers toward more abstract product evaluations, a change in psychological distance associated with lower returns. Managerial implications: Our findings reframe blockchain's value from backend efficiency to frontend consumer-behavior impact. Managers should treat BCT as a consumer-facing information channel that stabilizes the post-purchase decision: investment is most effective in experience-heavy categories where consumers can validate provenance against usage, while credence-heavy categories may require pairing BCT with third-party certifications. The validated language-model approach also gives operations managers a scalable tool to monitor consumer cognition from review text and calibrate transparency strategies by category.

detail.abstract: Faculty research productivity is an important dimension of higher-education performance, yet publication outcomes are shaped by more than individual research competence. This study diagnosed faculty research productivity through a systems-based analysis of secondary institutional data and developed a quality-improvement framework responsive to identified institutional gaps. A descriptive-analytical secondary-data research design was employed using institutional research and publication records. The analysis focused on faculty research engagement, completed research outputs, and publication in internationally refereed or Commission on Higher Education (CHED)-recognized journals. Root causes were subsequently organized using a Fishbone-based systems analysis covering people, process, resources, leadership, skills, collaboration, and research-to-impact factors. Results showed that 11 of 30 graduate-school faculty members (36.67%) were recorded as research-engaged, while 19 (63.33%) were not represented in the research-engaged group. A total of 920 research outputs were reported as completed in 2024. Within the specified publication dataset of 243 outputs, 51 (20.99%) were published in internationally refereed or CHED-recognized journals, leaving 192 outputs (79.01%) outside that publication category. The findings indicate two interconnected challenges: limited faculty participation in research and a substantial gap between research outputs and recognized scholarly publication. The study proposes a Systems-Based Research Quality Improvement Framework integrating faculty mentoring, publication acceleration, research support, capacity development, performance monitoring, research clusters, external partnerships, and research-toimpact translation. The study contributes a practical systems perspective for institutional research management and continuous quality improvement in higher education.

title: Teaching Generative AI Through Building: A Pedagogical Framework for Business Students
affiliations: University of Washington - Department of Information Systems and Operations Management

detail.title: Teaching Generative AI Through Building: A Pedagogical Framework for Business Students
detail.abstract: We present a pedagogical framework that teaches business students to build with, direct, and critically evaluate generative AI systems. The setting is a paired two-course sequence, five modules each, taught to two parallel cohorts of Master of Science in Information Systems (MSIS) students (N = 84) at the University of Washington Foster School of Business in Winter 2026. A fundamentals course ensures that every student, regardless of background, can do foundational technical work through an AI-assisted workflow. This paper documents the building course, which progresses from accelerating problem solving with AI, through creative problem solving and rapid prototyping ("vibe coding"), agentic systems and workflow orchestration, and human-AI decision-making and evaluation, to a capstone GenAI Fair with industry judges. Rather than treating AI as a subject to be studied, the framework treats it as a medium through which students develop core competencies: creative problem solving, critical thinking, rapid prototyping, AI direction, and evaluation judgment. Students develop capabilities as builders, orchestrators, and evaluators of AI systems, independent of their initial technical expertise. Evidence from two cohorts includes student-built portfolios, agentic workflows, industry-validated demonstrations at a public fair judged by alumni and industry leaders, and official course evaluations combining high ratings (combined medians of 4.9 and 4.8 of 5.0) with high reported challenge and workload. The framework is designed for replication: all assignments, teaching materials, and instructor-built tools are documented with open-source intent. This paper contributes a concrete, evidence-grounded model for teaching generative AI in business education, aligned to institutional AI learning outcomes.

title: Current Trends and The Importance of E-Journals

detail.title: Current Trends and The Importance of E-Journals

detail.abstract: This study examines the theoretical foundations, development trends, and technical requirements of electronic academic journal systems, and proposes a web-based platform for managing scholarly publications. It reviews the evolution of e-journals, open access, international indexing, and the growing role of artificial intelligence, and analyzes the principles of website architecture that underpin them. Based on a comparative analysis of existing systems-Open Journal Systems (OJS), Elsevier, and Springer-the study identifies the functional and non-functional requirements for an integrated journal management system. The proposed platform supports article submission, peer review, metadata management, PDF archiving, search, and secure access to improve the accessibility, transparency, and international competitiveness of academic journals.

title: The Limits of IAS/IFRS Standards in the Face of Artificial Intelligence in the Preparation, Analysis, Estimation, Measurement and Audit of Financial Information

detail.title: The Limits of IAS/IFRS Standards in the Face of Artificial Intelligence in the Preparation, Analysis, Estimation, Measurement and Audit of Financial Information
detail.abstract: This study critically examines the extent to which the International Accounting Standards / International Financial Reporting Standards (IAS/IFRS) framework — designed before the advent of modern artificial intelligence (AI) — remains adequate in an environment where machine-learning algorithms and generative AI systems now intervene in the preparation, estimation, measurement and audit of financial information. Drawing on six theoretical frameworks (agency theory, stakeholder theory, institutional theory, legitimacy theory, information-processing theory and algorithmic governance theory), the study identifies thirteen categories of structural limitations of IAS/IFRS in the face of AI, and then analyses in detail twelve standards (IFRS 9, IFRS 15, IFRS 16, IFRS 13, IAS 1, IAS 2, IAS 8, IAS 10, IAS 16, IAS 36, IAS 37, IAS 38) from the standpoint of the error, manipulation and noncompliance risks introduced by AI. Six scenarios of AI-assisted accounting manipulation are constructed and mapped to the standards concerned. The study also draws on real-world cases — Enron, Wirecard, Carillion, Silicon Valley Bank, Knight Capital, Zillow Offers, as well as the SEC's first enforcement actions against "AI-washing" — to illustrate, without anachronism, both the continuity and the discontinuity between "classic" governance failures and risks that are specifically algorithmic in nature. The insufficiencies of the ISA auditing standards with respect to the audit of AI systems are then examined, before proposing a fourlayer integrated governance model (IAS/IFRS – ISA – algorithmic governance – continuous audit) and a conceptual research model linking AI adoption, algorithmic transparency and financial information quality. The study concludes that IAS/IFRS, being principles-based and therefore in theory technologically neutral, nonetheless suffer from a specific operational deficit in the face of opacity, data dependency and the absence of algorithmic traceability — a deficit that calls for a body of complementary application guidance rather than a wholesale overhaul of the framework.

title:
The One-Number Temptation

When a Single Measure Earns the Right to Govern a Complex System

detail.title:
The One-Number Temptation

When a Single Measure Earns the Right to Govern a Complex System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: Every discipline reaches for a single number supposed to govern a complex system: the order parameter, the basic reproduction number, the biomarker, the test score. Some of these reductions are triumphs. Others have been the opposite, some with lethal consequences. The claim concerns institutional practice rather than professed belief: no clinician holds that a biomarker is the disease, and particular surrogates have nonetheless been accepted, in trial design and in clinical use, as though an effect on the marker were an effect on the outcome. The same substitution occurs wherever a score or a ranking is used to allocate what it was built only to describe. What separates the reductions that hold from those that fail is not arithmetic. A one-dimensional encoding of any finitely represented system always exists, so finding one proves nothing. What licenses a reduction is mechanism. The physical and mathematical sciences supply three paradigms — timescale separation, threshold proximity, a binding constraint — each stating in advance why one dimension suffices and when it will cease to. Disciplines that borrowed the practice without the precondition rediscovered the consequence separately, under local names: the committor problem, overdispersion, surrogate-endpoint failure, the Lucas critique and Goodhart's law, reification. The mechanisms of failure differ; the error of judgment is one. The essay proposes four delimiters and a protocol for adjudicating scalar claims prospectively, specified formally in the appendices together with the Scalar Conjecture the protocol exists to test. The protocol has not been run against systems of known structure, and until it is, it remains a proposal about method. Its own defeat condition is stated in advance.

detail.abstract: This article examines the rise of India’s Generation Z movement through the case of the Cockroach Janata Party and argues that its rapid expansion cannot be understood without considering the political power of social-media algorithms. It explains how changes to Instagram’s recommendation system after 2024 enabled a new and previously unknown account to reach millions of users without an established follower base, media network, or political organisation. At the same time, it argues that the same algorithmic system that amplifies a movement can also make it nearly invisible by reducing its reach without deleting posts or formally suspending accounts. Drawing on examples from the United States, Vietnam, Turkey, China, and India, the article examines how governments and technology companies use content moderation, throttling, recommendation policies, regulatory pressure, and commercial incentives to shape political visibility. It also analyses the unequal enforcement of platform policies in India and the limited transparency surrounding political recommendation systems. The article concludes that movements built primarily on privately controlled digital platforms remain structurally vulnerable because their access to supporters depends on corporate algorithms. It therefore calls for independent communication networks, including websites, email lists, consent-based phone databases, and decentralised organisational structures.

title: Cognitive Offloading and the Human-Feedback Channel: Why RLHF Preference Judgments Are the Untested Link Between Human Cognitive Decline and AI Training Quality
affiliations: and Injibara University

detail.title: Cognitive Offloading and the Human-Feedback Channel: Why RLHF Preference Judgments Are the Untested Link Between Human Cognitive Decline and AI Training Quality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Two research directions are converging. One shows heavy AI use is linked to weaker critical thinking. The other builds formal models coupling human cognition and AI training as one system. Both assume degraded human input lowers AI training quality in general. Neither tests a specific, high-leverage channel: reinforcement learning from human feedback, where people directly judge which AI output is better. This is a distinct cognitive task from writing or search, closer to comparison and discrimination than generation. We argue cognitive offloading may degrade this judgment specifically, which would lower training signal quality at scale. We review the Data Wall and model collapse literature, the cognitive offloading literature, and recent coupled-system models, and show precisely where this literature stops short of testing the RLHF channel. We propose a concrete, feasible study design to test it. This is a narrow, testable hypothesis and a runnable protocol, not a new general theory.

title: Access And Control: Artificial Intelligence, Dual Secrecy, And The Freedom To Tinker
affiliations: Elon University School of Law

detail.title: Access And Control: Artificial Intelligence, Dual Secrecy, And The Freedom To Tinker

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No financial or other relationship with any named entities.
declarations.funderStatement: Supported by a research grant from Elon University School of Law.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming, Elgar Research Handbook on Trade Secrecy in Data and Data Infrastructure, 2026.

detail.abstract:
The era of artificial intelligence and its cataclysmic subgenre, generative artificial intelligence (“GenAI,” collectively “AI”), began suddenly on November 30, 2022, when OpenAI unilaterally released ChatGPT for public consumption and use. Its immediate impact has created new opportunities for expression and innovation while provoking fundamental questions about what it means to be human—and about what brings joy and meaning to life while paying the bills. Thoughtful, balanced, and humane answers to these questions require access to information and an understanding of AI by those who do not profit directly from maximizing its sales and use. Trade secrecy stands as a barrier to that access and understanding.

This chapter identifies and analyzes AI’s “dual secrecy” problem. It begins with dual challenges. On one side, AI customers risk losing legal protection for their trade secrets through GenAI inputs and outputs. On the other hand, AI providers invoke trade secrecy to prevent customers, governments, and the public from accessing the information necessary to understand how AI systems work and hold them accountable. AI thus creates new methods for generating, losing, disseminating, and leaking trade secrets while maintaining its own secrets behind a legal and technological wall.

The result is a proverbial house of mirrors. AI is a siren that offers quick, easy, and inexpensive content and analysis, but when used carelessly, it can reveal or misuse a company’s trade secret crown jewels. At the same time, AI remains a black box whose code, training data, and decision-making processes often cannot be meaningfully examined, replicated, or explained—even by those with internal access. The combination of trade secrecy and technological complexity therefore creates information bottlenecks across AI’s entire use spectrum.

These bottlenecks are particularly pernicious when governments procure and deploy privately developed AI systems. Secrecy between private providers and government combines with secrecy between government and the public, producing “dual secrecy” throughout the government information ecosystem. The resulting blind spots invite error, manipulation, weak or no accountability, unintended consequences, real and imagined concerns, and suboptimal use of expensive systems acquired with taxpayer dollars.

This chapter is the first to examine this dual secrecy problem in detail. It proposes a tailored “freedom to tinker” that would permit appropriate examination, testing, and optimization of AI systems, particularly when they are procured for public use. Such freedom is necessary to protect proprietary information while enabling accountable AI, meaningful oversight, and informed public understanding. The result might render AI a true tool for public good, rather than a murky black box that creates concerns and risks that can eclipse its benefits.

title: Internal Auditors as Architects of AI-Ready Enterprise Data Governance: Enabling Structure through ISO 21378 and ISO/TS 21377
affiliations: , The College of New Jersey and Rutgers Business School

detail.title: Internal Auditors as Architects of AI-Ready Enterprise Data Governance: Enabling Structure through ISO 21378 and ISO/TS 21377
detail.abstract: Despite massive investment in Generative AI (GenAI), 80% to 95% of enterprise projects fail (MIT NANDA, 2025), stalling in the "pilot graveyard" due to data infrastructure deficiencies (Deloitte, 2026). Legacy ERP environments suffer from Semantic Entropy: the fragmentation of data definitions, localized customizations, and human entry discrepancies that confuse probabilistic algorithms and fuel financial hallucinations. To bridge this gap, organizations must move away from a blind reliance on data volume and establish a deterministic, pre-validated ingestion layer. This paper introduces a data governance framework that transforms the internal auditor from a retrospective reviewer into a proactive Data Steward. Leveraging ISO 21378 as a universal semantic dictionary and ISO/TS 21377 for interoperable technical packaging, internal auditors can construct an unalterable "Buffer of Truth." The proposed AIready data ecosystem insulates generative models from semantic drift, ensuring hallucination-free enterprise AI deployment.

title: Factual Grounding and Response Calibration as Distinct Reliability - Challenges in Agentic AI Systems: An Enterprise Case Study

detail.title: Factual Grounding and Response Calibration as Distinct Reliability - Challenges in Agentic AI Systems: An Enterprise Case Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently with no financial relationships with external organizations that could influence the study.

No human participants, patient data, or personally identifiable information were involved. Ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Enterprise deployments of AI systems face two reliability challenges that are frequently studied in isolation: ensuring generated responses are grounded in verified source material, and ensuring response format and depth match what a user actually asked. This paper reports a longitudinal case study of an agentic AI system developed for enterprise contract risk analysis, tracing its development across four iterative versions over approximately three weeks. We investigate whether factual grounding and response calibration, the appropriateness of response scope and depth relative to user intent, function as separable reliability dimensions requiring distinct engineering interventions. Holding a retrievalgrounded knowledge architecture constant across all four versions, we document how response calibration evolved only after the explicit introduction of intent classification at the prompt level. Early versions without intent classification returned either uniformly comprehensive responses regardless of query specificity, or uniformly minimal responses lacking necessary context. The final version, incorporating explicit intent classification, produced responses appropriately scoped to distinct query types. This paper offers empirical evidence from a single longitudinal case suggesting that grounding and response calibration may represent separable reliability dimensions, presented as a hypothesis for future controlled, multi-system research rather than a generalized claim.

title: Do People Actually Listen? A Survey on Email Security Awareness and Communication Strategies
affiliations: Hacks/Hackers

detail.title: Do People Actually Listen? A Survey on Email Security Awareness and Communication Strategies
detail.abstract: This research paper aims to identify and evaluate the best practices for email security, assess the effectiveness of communication and awareness strategies used to promote email security among end-users, and explore the factors that influence end- user behavior towards email security best practices. The research design included a comprehensive literature review of the latest trends, strategies, and technologies used to mitigate email security risks, as well as a survey-based empirical study of end-users. The findings suggest that while many end-users are aware of email security risks, there is still a significant lack of understanding and adoption of best practices for mitigating these risks. Effective communication and awareness strategies, such as email security training and education, software and tools, and company-wide policies, can promote email security awareness and adoption among end-users. The study highlights the importance of effective communication and awareness strategies to promote email security awareness and adoption among end-users, and provides insights into the factors that influence end-user behavior towards email security best practices. The recommendations for improving email security awareness and adoption among end-users include investing in email security training and education programs, software and tools, and company-wide policies to mitigate email security risks.

detail.abstract: Online retailers increasingly use recommendation cues to guide consumer attention and reduce search effort, yet less is known about whether the stated source of a recommendation changes consumer response. This study tested dynamic recommendation source framing: the idea that firms may improve recommendation effectiveness by matching the stated source of a recommendation to the product context. In a 2 × 4 betweensubjects experiment, 185 participants viewed one fictional Shoply product page featuring either a portable charger or a hoodie and one of four recommendation-source conditions: AI shopping assistant, product expert, customers with similar preferences, or no label. After excluding five participants who failed product recall, the final analytic sample included 180 participants. The product-type manipulation worked strongly: the charger was perceived as more objective/performance-based, and the hoodie was perceived as more taste/style-based. Product type significantly affected purchase intention and perceived personalization, but recommendation source did not significantly affect purchase intention, trust, or perceived personalization. The expected Product Type × Recommendation Source interaction was also not supported. Source recall was low, with half of participants selecting "I don't remember" when asked which recommendation source appeared. These findings suggest that subtle recommendation-source labels may be less influential than product context unless the source cue is salient, diagnostic, and clearly connected to product relevance. The study contributes a boundary condition for dynamic recommendation source framing and offers practical implications for e-commerce explanation design.
