title: Room to Breathe: The Surprising Capaciousness of OSH Act Preemption
affiliations: Saint Louis University School of Law

detail.title: Room to Breathe: The Surprising Capaciousness of OSH Act Preemption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

publicationDetails.detailsText: Saint Louis U. Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Saint Louis University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This essay is part of a Saint Louis University Law Journal seminar, conducted by the Wefel Center for Employment Law, titled "Shifting Workplace Law in an Era of Federal Vacuums: Business as Usual or Polycrisis?" The symposium presumed that the federal government would be scaling back workforce regulatory enforcement dramatically in the shadow of DOGE and several other developments. The essay focuses on OSHA and more narrowly questions the extent to which the OSH Act preempts state and local efforts to regulate workplace safety and health. The essay shows that unless OSHA promulgates a full-blown “standard” – a tedious form of notice and comment rulemaking that corporate interests famously frustrate through sometimes decades-long process – OSHA cannot block state and local workplace safety regulation at all. The essay recounts some of the legislative history surrounding the enactment of the OSH Act. The history helps to explain the restricted preemption provisions in the OSH Act that are much more forgiving than aggressive NLRA or ERISA preemption. While this relative relaxation was the product of states’ rights insisted upon by republican elements within Congress and the Nixon Administration, circa 1969, it may produce unexpected impacts in the current political environment. For example, if corporate interests frustrate issuance of a worker “heat rule,” currently tied up within OSHA as of this writing, states (whether or not possessing OSHA-authorized “state plans”) are at complete liberty to issue heat regulation that is more aggressive than anything “federal OSHA” might be expected to devise.  

 The essay introduces New York City’s recent heat rules as an example of state or local workplace safety and health law created in reaction to a perceived lapse of federal workplace safety and health regulation. It distinguishes New York City’s heat rules from New York State’s “ergonomics rules” (another area of perceived workplace safety and health regulatory lapse) for the purpose of explaining how the existence of an OSHA “standard” drives OSH Act preemption. It further distinguishes the analysis of preemption involving dual-impact state laws, purporting to regulate both public and workplace safety and health risks, from “typical” state/federal OSH Act conflict. The essay discusses preemption mechanisms in other federal labor and employment statutes and argues that the OSH Act leaves more state law discretion than the other statutes, which in the context of the present moment, “feels different.” The essay concludes that OSH Act preemption, while imperfect, is (in context) preferrable to other forms of preemption, is arguably consistent with Congressional intent, and provides at least some room under state and local law for protecting worker safety and health during a long night of federal retreat.

title: Who Authors Our Minds? Brain-Computer Interfaces, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of Copyright
affiliations: Fordham University, School of Law and Fordham Law School

detail.title: Who Authors Our Minds? Brain-Computer Interfaces, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of Copyright
detail.abstract:
Abstract

Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) are transforming the relationship among human cognition, artificial intelligence, and copyright law. Once confined to laboratory research, implantable BCIs have entered human clinical trials and can increasingly decode task-specific neural activity into text, speech, images, commands, and other externally perceptible outputs. When combined with AI systems capable of interpreting, refining, and fixing neural signals into expressive works, BCIs challenge one of copyright law’s foundational assumptions: that ideas remain legally unprotected until a human author voluntarily externalizes them as original expression fixed in a tangible medium.

BCIs disrupt this conventional sequence. Neural activity may be captured, decoded, transformed, and fixed through substantial technological mediation. The human user may supply the intellectual conception, while algorithms determine meaning, expressive form, and the final embodiment of the work. This raises two questions copyright doctrine has never squarely confronted: who, if anyone, authors a work derived directly from neural activity, and when does human cognition become legally cognizable expression?

This Article argues that existing doctrine is structurally ill-equipped to answer those questions. The fixation requirement, the idea–expression dichotomy, and traditional theories of human authorship were developed for a world in which internal thought and external expression were separated by a deliberate act of writing, speaking, recording, or performance. BCIs erode that separation. If decoded neural outputs are categorically treated as unprotectable ideas, individuals may be exposed to the unauthorized appropriation and commercialization of their cognitive contributions. Yet recognizing rights in all decoded neural activity risks converting unformed or involuntary thought into alienable property, chilling freedom of thought and impeding research and innovation. Allowing ownership to default to the entity controlling the decoding infrastructure would instead transform technological power into a proxy for authorship.

The Article first examines whether decoded neural outputs can satisfy copyright’s threshold requirements of originality, human authorship, and fixation. It then evaluates competing ownership claims. Neurotechnology developers may assert rights based on control over fixation, selection and arrangement, technological and financial investment, Lockean labor theory, and innovation incentives. The human user, however, may claim authorship based on intellectual conception, biological and cognitive individuality, personality theory, autonomy, and moral accountability. The analysis draws on the U.S. Copyright Office’s 2025 report, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability, and the litigation culminating in the Supreme Court’s 2026 denial of certiorari in Thaler v. Perlmutter.

Neither position can be adopted categorically. Corporate investment does not itself establish copyright authorship, while neural origin alone does not make every decoded output protectable expression. The analysis must also remain bounded by constitutional and human-rights constraints, including freedom of thought, mental privacy, cognitive liberty, bodily autonomy, and psychological integrity. Consent is essential, but it regulates permission rather than authorship or title.

The Article’s central contribution is a new Neuro-IP framework: a purpose-limited, consent-anchored, and phase-sensitive regime that distinguishes internal cognition, raw neural data, decoded content, AI-mediated transformation, and final fixed expression. Internal thought remains outside copyright. Protection arises only when neural activity becomes sufficiently original, externally perceptible, and fixed expression attributable to human creative contribution. Rights are then allocated according to intellectual conception, expressive control, technological transformation, and the scope of voluntary consent.

The central question is therefore not whether copyright should protect thought as such. It should not. The question is when cognition mediated by BCIs and AI crosses the legal threshold from unprotectable idea to copyrightable expression. Neurotechnology changes what can be decoded and fixed. Copyright must adapt to protect human creativity without enclosing the mind itself.

title: Risk Factors and Clinical Pathways of Stillbirth in Gauteng, South Africa: A Retrospective Hospital-Based Studyinter
affiliations: University of Johannesburg

detail.title: Risk Factors and Clinical Pathways of Stillbirth in Gauteng, South Africa: A Retrospective Hospital-Based Studyinter

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval:
Ethical approval for this retrospective study using routinely collected maternity records was obtained from Wits postgraduate ethics committee. (reference number: 737079/2020. Permission to access and analyse the records was obtained from Department of Health. Data were de-identified before analysis and handled in accordance with applicable ethical and data-protection requirements.

 Patient Consent: Individual informed consent was waived by the ethics review committee because this study involved retrospective analysis of de-identified routinely collected clinical records and posed minimal risk to participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Background: Stillbirth remains a major public-health concern in South Africa. Evidence from routine hospital records that jointly examines maternal, fetal, placental, umbilical-cord and care-related characteristics is limited.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective comparative study using routinely collected maternity records from selected Gauteng hospitals between June 2023 and 2024. The analytical dataset comprised 18,672 birth records: 512 stillbirths and 18,160 live births. The outcome was coded as live birth (1) and stillbirth (0). We used descriptive statistics, group-difference tests and progressively adjusted non-linear logistic-regression models. Free-text documented causes among stillbirths were re-coded into hypertensive/placental disorders, fetal growth restriction or hypoxia, infection, congenital abnormality, maternal medical/metabolic disorder, obstetric/labour complication, unexplained, and excluded/missing categories.

Results: Stillbirths were associated with lower fetal weight and earlier gestation than live births. In adjusted models, hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and selected fetal, placental and umbilical-cord characteristics were associated with lower odds of live birth. Fetal weight, gestational age and maternal age showed non-linear associations with the odds of live birth. Hypertensive and placental disorders were commonly documented among stillbirths and frequently co-occurred with fetal growth restriction, hypoxia, infection and maternal medical conditions. Infection was prominent in descriptive cause classifications but was not independently associated with the outcome in the final adjusted model.

Conclusion: In these selected Gauteng hospitals, stillbirth was associated with interacting maternal, fetal, placental, infectious and care-related characteristics. The findings support strengthened antenatal booking, fetal-growth surveillance, management of hypertension, diabetes and infection, and timely obstetric response to suspected placental or cord complications. Owing to the retrospective design and use of routine clinical records, the findings represent associations and should not be interpreted as causal effects.

reference: UCLA School of Law Working Paper
title: The New Vertically Integrated Utility
affiliations: University of Chicago - Law School

detail.title: The New Vertically Integrated Utility

publicationDetails.detailsText: UCLA School of Law Working Paper

detail.abstract: Domestic electricity demand is growing for the first time in decades, driven by energy-intensive data centers, reshoring of industry, and broad electrification. Regulatory hurdles and supply chain constraints render electricity supply highly inelastic in the near term. In an electricity-constrained environment, utilities have become attractive acquisition targets for well-resourced large-load electricity customers and their owners. Such acquisitions create vertically integrated firms that operate in both competitive and monopolistic markets. Vertical integration of this sort raises antitrust concerns. Yet so far, the prevailing assumption has been that state and federal regulatory agencies, together with antitrust law, are sufficient to guard the public interest against problematic vertical mergers. This Article shows that the modern iteration of vertical integration allows utilities to circumvent these guardrails. Forward vertical integration, a form of integration wherein a rate-regulated utility merges with a downstream large-load customer, creates perverse incentives for utilities to advantage their affiliate customer through (1) service prioritization; (2) changed procurement decisions; and (3) risk-shifting onto other customer classes. Utilities can pursue these ends through what regulators see as ordinary business decisions, rather than through the ratemaking process regulators are equipped to scrutinize. As such, regulators will struggle to rein in this non-price discrimination. This new form of vertical integration unmasks a persistent problem in integrated regulated monopolies: the ability to transfer value towards unregulated affiliates through ordinary business decisions, which regulators defer to. Concurrently, modern antitrust doctrine surrounding this form of vertical integration suffers from a similar myopia by focusing primarily on price discrimination. Absent a recognition of utilities' ability to transfer value to affiliates without altering prices, antitrust is ill-prepared to guard the public interest. To prevent harm to consumers and competition, this Article proposes a set of solutions for regulators and courts to adopt. Specifically, the Article proposes that regulators require mitigating measures prior to merger approval; that FERC broaden its § 203 review to account for downstream consequences of forward mergers; that state PUCs broaden their definition of what constitutes "the public interest"; and that courts embrace a modernized antitrust posture that recognizes the unique market abuses made possible by forward vertical integration.

title: Economic Development, Health Awareness, and Bariatric Healthcare Supply as Drivers of Obesity Dynamics: A 195-Country Panel Analysis With Regional Application to China
affiliations: Shanxi Provincial People's Hospital, Shanxi Bethune Hospital, Shanxi Bethune Hospital, Shanxi Bethune Hospital, Shanxi Bethune Hospital, Shanxi Bethune Hospital, Shanxi Bethune Hospital and Shanxi Bethune Hospital

detail.title: Economic Development, Health Awareness, and Bariatric Healthcare Supply as Drivers of Obesity Dynamics: A 195-Country Panel Analysis With Regional Application to China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Background: The drivers of global obesity extend beyond diet and economic growth—yet the roles of health awareness (proxied by media attention) and bariatric healthcare supply have not been integrated into a unified macro-ecological framework. This study quantifies the triadic influence of economic development, dietary intake, media-driven health awareness, and bariatric surgery provision on obesity dynamics across 195 countries, and applies the model to generate regionally differentiated policy guidance for China.

Methods: We assembled a panel dataset spanning 195 countries from 1980 to 2024, integrating five data sources: WHO Global Health Observatory (age-standardised obesity prevalence), World Bank (GDP per capita), FAO Food Balance Sheets (dietary energy supply), IFSO Global Registry Reports (bariatric procedures per million), and a constructed health-news interest index from Google Trends and GDELT. Eight model specifications were compared. The primary specification models annual changes in obesity prevalence (Δ-obesity) via random forest, eliminating autoregressive dominance. Scenario simulations projected 15-year trajectories under baseline and policy-counterfactual conditions. China was analysed across seven geographic macro-regions.

Findings: Among eight candidate models, those incorporating the lagged dependent variable achieved R²>0.999 but were discarded because obesity_lag1 dominated feature importance (>89%). The primary Δ-obesity model (R²=0.29, RMSE=0.24 pp/yr) identified GDP×health-news interaction as the strongest predictor (importance=18.0%), followed by 3-year-lagged dietary intake (16.7%) and GDP×bariatric-surgery interaction (14.0%). Mixed-effects modelling confirmed an inverted-U GDP–obesity relationship (ln[GDP] β=+18.57, p<0.001; ln[GDP]² β=−0.77, p<0.001). China has an obesity prevalence of 9.3%—18.6 percentage points below its income-group expectation—but its annual growth rate has accelerated from +0.09 pp/yr (1990–2000) to +0.50 pp/yr (2020–2024). Sub-national analysis identified Central China (0.51 pp/yr), North China, and Northeast China as first-priority intervention regions.

Interpretation: China's obesity prevalence remains remarkably low for its income level, but accelerating growth signals a narrowing policy window. The interaction between economic development and health-news penetration is the strongest predictor of obesity change, implying that public health campaigns yield greater marginal returns during middle-income transitions. Region-specific intervention packages are urgently needed.

reference: Columbia Business School Research Paper Forthcoming
title: Visa Access and the Geography of Skilled Work: Evidence from the H-1B Lottery
affiliations: University of Wyoming - College of Business and Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: Visa Access and the Geography of Skilled Work: Evidence from the H-1B Lottery

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Business School Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We compare H-1B lottery winners and losers, matching administrative lottery records to LinkedIn career histories and US patent applications. We use random lottery selection as an instrument for receiving a visa. Whether losing the initial lottery has lasting effects depends on workers' ability to reach US employment through other routes and on whether worker-firm matches can be preserved abroad. Over three to six years, receiving a visa raises the probability of starting a US job by 2.4 percentage points, yet 65.7% of registrants who lose their initial H-1B lottery eventually start a US job. Failing to receive a visa also raises the probability of starting a foreign position at a US-headquartered company by 1.7 percentage points, a 44% increase relative to the 3.8% mean, including positions within the sponsor's corporate family. Receiving a visa also affects early careers, raising annual salary by 6.7% and the likelihood of filing a patent application by 38%. We interpret these estimates as evidence on where the frictions associated with the H-1B lottery bind. H-1B access changes where some worker-firm matches are realized and affects early-career outcomes, while adjustment through other routes allows most initial lottery losers eventually to start a US job.

title: Geographic Clustering of Immunization Risk in Sierra Leone: A Facility-Based Geospatial and Health-Systems Analysis Across 16 Districts
affiliations: Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation, Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation, Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation, Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation, Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation, Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation, Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation, Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation, Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation and Government of Sierra Leone - Ministry of Health and Sanitation

detail.title: Geographic Clustering of Immunization Risk in Sierra Leone: A Facility-Based Geospatial and Health-Systems Analysis Across 16 Districts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval for the supportive supervision exercise and secondary data analysis was obtained from the Expanded Program on Immunization-Ministry of Health. All data were anonymised before analysis, and confidentiality was maintained throughout the study.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Background: Despite high national childhood immunisation coverage in Sierra Leone, subnational disparities continue to leave communities at risk of under-immunisation and zero-dose status. Understanding the geographic distribution of immunisation risk and the health-system factors associated with these disparities is essential for designing targeted interventions. This study assessed the spatial clustering of facility-level immunisation risk and compared programme and health-system characteristics between hotspot and non-hotspot districts across Sierra Leone.

Methods: A nationwide cross-sectional geospatial and health-systems analysis was conducted using supportive supervision data from 249 routine immunisation facilities across all 16 districts of Sierra Leone. A composite immunisation risk score (0-9) was constructed from three indicators of under-immunisation risk and categorised into low, medium, and high risk. Global Moran's I and Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) identified spatial clustering and hotspot districts. Descriptive statistics summarised programme characteristics, while Pearson's Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests compared health-system indicators between hotspot and non-hotspot districts at a significance level of p<0.05.

Results: Of the 249 facilities, 68.7% were classified as low risk, 18.1% as medium risk, and 13.3% as high risk. Immunisation risk demonstrated significant spatial clustering (Global Moran's I=0.223; permutation p=0.001). Western Area Urban (mean risk score=3.7; 46.7% high-risk facilities) and Bonthe (2.5; 43.8%) exhibited the highest risk, with Western Area Rural (2.1; 26.7%) also showing elevated risk. Hotspot districts had significantly higher availability of updated routine immunisation micro plans (48.4% vs. 13.3%, p<0.001), recent funding (90.3% vs. 69.7%, p<0.001), and supervisory visits (77.4% vs. 56.0%, p<0.001), but were more likely to report insufficient funding (96.4% vs. 85.5%, p=0.02) and lower community health worker assignment (83.9% vs. 95.0%, p=0.002).

Conclusion: Immunisation risk in Sierra Leone is geographically clustered rather than randomly distributed, with distinct hotspots concentrated in Western Area Urban, Western Area Rural, and Bonthe. Integrating geospatial analysis into routine immunisation monitoring can facilitate precision public health approaches by enabling targeted resource allocation, strengthening community outreach, and reducing geographical inequities in immunisation coverage.

title: Supply-Driven Inflation and Exchange-Rate Policy: Evidence from Singapore
affiliations: Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation

detail.title: Supply-Driven Inflation and Exchange-Rate Policy: Evidence from Singapore
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether changes in inflation dynamics following the COVID-19 pandemic were accompanied by changes in monetary policy behaviour in a highly open economy, using Singapore as a case study. We combine a split-sample sign-restricted structural vector autoregression with the first ordered probit model of Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) policy decisions. The structural analysis shows that global oil supply shocks became substantially more important drivers of core inflation after the pandemic, while the contribution of domestic demand declined. Despite this structural shift, the ordered probit results indicate that the output gap remains the strongest predictor of policy decisions, whereas medium-term movements in the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S\$NEER) provide additional explanatory power beyond inflation and real activity. These findings suggest that changes in inflation dynamics need not be accompanied by comparable changes in monetary policy behaviour. More broadly, the paper demonstrates how combining structural and discrete-choice models provides complementary evidence on monetary policy transmission in highly open economies.

title: The FICO Blind Spot: Why LLMs Hallucinate When Credit Gets Real

detail.title: The FICO Blind Spot: Why LLMs Hallucinate When Credit Gets Real
detail.abstract: The FICO score, dominant for six decades, is structurally incapable of assessing the 32 million credit-invisible adults in the United States and approximately 3 billion individuals globally who lack sufficient traditional credit histories. A rapidly maturing ecosystem of alternative credit data-cash flow signals, rent and utility histories, gig platform earnings, digital behavioral footprints, and cross-border credit portability-is filling this gap, with the alternative credit scoring market projected to grow from $1.5 billion in 2025 to $11.7 billion by 2035 at a 23.1% CAGR. Large Language Models are now being deployed to reason over this data at scale. Yet benchmark data reveals a critical problem: LLMs hallucinate between 15% and 52% of the time on structured financial analysis tasks, with four out of six leading models fabricating financial data when faced with incomplete source documents. This paper presents the first comprehensive analysis pairing each failure mode with documented market solutions. We introduce the Alternative Credit Hallucination Taxonomy (ACHT)-mapping six alternative data types to specific LLM compliance failure modes-and counterbalance each failure mode with solutions from Experian, Upstart, Zest AI, Nova Credit, Moody's AI Studio, Alloy, and Credolab. We analyse provider-level, platform-level, and ROI constraints, and present a seven-layer reference architecture incorporating deterministic pre-processing engines, ECOA proxy filters, and Deployment Half-Life (DHL) governance.

title: Right Before the News: Prediction Markets and the Assets They Reference

detail.title: Right Before the News: Prediction Markets and the Assets They Reference

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author operates live, capital-committed systematic trading strategies on Polymarket, the venue studied in this paper. The author held no equity, option, or derivative position in the specific single-stock tickers examined in the paper, nor in TLT, SPY, or QQQ, during the sample periods analyzed (2024-07 through 2026-07), beyond incidental passive exposure through standard diversified retail holdings. The author has no institutional, advisory, or consulting relationship with Polymarket, Kalshi, Deribit, Pinnacle, or any brokerage or data vendor whose data is used in this paper, and received no funding, compensation, data access, or other in-kind benefit from any of them in connection with this research. The paper's best-powered results were conducted under pre-registered protocols fixed before outcomes were examined, and its headline corrections run against the narrative that would most favor the venue the author trades on; the interest is disclosed in full so readers can weigh it themselves.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All data subscriptions were self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: A growing practitioner narrative treats prediction-market odds as a fast alt-data signal that "leads" the assets they reference. We test this at minute resolution, under newswire-verified timestamps and pre-registered protocols, with every deviation logged (Appendix A). The signature we find is anticipation, not speed. In the largest single outcome across 64 measured single-stock corporate events, Polymarket was already at least 80% priced on the correct side before the news existed (28 events). On earnings, these pre-event prices beat trailing-history and climatology benchmarks (exploratory) and match forecasters anchored on the recorded analyst consensus; on FDA decisions they match the published approval base rate. A naive strategy of buying the stock on Polymarket's confidence lost money on 17 of 22 trades in our sample (ruling out a naive edge, no more); the anticipation is an information result, not an equity trading signal. The reaction race itself is statistically indistinguishable: 12 stock-led, 11 Polymarket-led, and 9 inside the one-minute resolution floor, with post-hoc bounds excluding only gross splits (beyond roughly 73/27); a seconds-scale lead remains untested. A pre-registered 18-cell macro test finds nothing significant, and the post-release convergence trade loses 72–82% of stake. The narrative's one academic anchor, a reported daily lead of Polymarket's election odds over DJT stock, does not reproduce on its own specification (headline Granger p=0.27; the instrument's first stage fails); what survives is overnight absorption: the opening gap prices what the 24/7 venue absorbed while the exchange was shut, a channel no trader can transact ahead of. Prediction markets arrive at the right price before events happen; nothing we measured shows them beating other markets to it.

title: Adverse Selection and the Government Intervention Trap *
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Adverse Selection and the Government Intervention Trap *

contentType.other: conditionally accepted , Review of Financial Studies

detail.abstract: In a dynamic setting, high-quality firms may tolerate current adverse selection when raising financing because they expect future opportunities to profitably acquire assets from failed lower-quality firms. But search frictions in asset trading impede efficiency, inviting government intervention. Anticipation of such intervention affects ex ante adverse selection and project investment because it reduces buyers' ex post trading profits. Depending on parameter values, this anticipation can have either pernicious or salutary effects. The pernicious effect reduces participation by high-quality firms, worsens adverse selection, and depresses project investment, potentially triggering investment-enhancing government assistance (an "intervention trap"). The salutary effect mitigates adverse selection and increases project investment.

title: Adverse Labor Market Shocks and Entrepreneurship
affiliations: West Virginia University

detail.title: Adverse Labor Market Shocks and Entrepreneurship
detail.abstract: In this study, I examine the effects of adverse labor market shocks on business entry. Exploiting variation in the severity of recessions across commuting zones, I find that severe labor market shocks persistently reduce employer establishment entry, implying that the increased financial constraints faced by potential entrepreneurs outweigh the "unemployment push" effects. I then propose a shift-share instrumental variable to examine the cyclicality of business entry. I find substantial heterogeneity that entrepreneurship exhibits procyclical patterns during the Great Recession and the subsequent period, but countercyclical patterns during the China Shock period.

title: Measuring the Economic Value of Employment: A Shift-Share Decomposition of Social Security Contribution Bases in Spain (2018-2025)

detail.title: Measuring the Economic Value of Employment: A Shift-Share Decomposition of Social Security Contribution Bases in Spain (2018-2025)
detail.abstract:
Purpose-Between 2004 and 2025 the Spanish labour market went through a lost decade, needing twelve years to recover its initial employment level, followed by an expansion without recent precedent. This paper examines whether the second decade improved not only the quantity but also the quality of employment, understood as its added value, and draws the implications for the sustainability of the contributory pension system. 

Design/methodology/approach-The paper exploits a source seldom used in the literature: the average contribution base by economic activity published by the Social Security General Treasury (Tesorería General de la Seguridad Social, TGSS). An exact shift-share decomposition separates the change in the aggregate average base into a composition effect (employment shifts across activities) and a price effect (base growth within activities), in nominal and real terms. 

Findings-Virtually all the improvement in the average base (28.9% in 2018-2025) stems from the price effect, itself mostly inflation; the composition effect is 0.26 percentage points. Net job creation split almost evenly between high-base and low-base activities. Record contribution revenue (+70.7%) coexisted with a persistent contributory deficit covered by growing State transfers, so the sustainability problem shifts from the composition of revenues towards expenditure and demography. 

Originality/value-The average contribution base by activity provides a direct operational measure of the value of employment for the contributory system, replacing the indirect inference of earlier literature with an explicit quantification of the composition and price channels.

title: Managing a Construction Engineering Project: Principles and Examples
affiliations: and National Taiwan University

detail.title: Managing a Construction Engineering Project: Principles and Examples
detail.abstract: Administering a construction project isn't just telling the staff what to do; it's making sure each piece of the domino falls right after the one before it, creating the full domino effect, otherwise known as project delivery. Construction administration is a critical phase in the life of a construction project. It bridges the gap between design and execution. It encompasses coordinating materials, scheduling, fund management, and contract regulation, and aims to maintain quality and efficiency throughout. Administering construction projects involves meticulous collaboration with architects, owners, subcontractors, and contractors to address risks and find ways to deal with challenges so the project is completed on time and on budget. The most pivotal role of construction administration is documenting and problem-solving throughout the process. The three key factors that stand out most among the numerous tasks an administrator does are risk management, problem-solving, and budget oversight. It's up to the project administrator to determine which leap of faith is worth it for complete project delivery. Staying on track is one of the biggest obstacles in every construction project. With timely solutions, the administrator addresses issues and solves problems as they arise. Lastly, budget constraints are vital to a project's successful completion. The administrator oversees and monitors project expenses while managing financial resources to ensure the project stays within the allowed limit. In a fast-paced construction world, the road from step one to a completed project is far from smooth. As easy as it may look on paper, the challenge comes from navigating the issues that arise during project administration. What will be next? New technology to adopt? Tighter margins for budgets?

title: Economic Freedom and Health: How robust is the positive association, and what do we actually learn?
affiliations: Lund University - Department of Economics, Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN)

detail.title: Economic Freedom and Health: How robust is the positive association, and what do we actually learn?
detail.abstract: Economic-freedom research has focused heavily on GDP, income, and growth. This paper asks whether the policies of economic freedom are also associated with outcomes closer to lived welfare, and whether economic freedom should be understood as part of the broader socio-economic processes through which countries improve population health. It combines the chain-linked \emph{Economic Freedom of the World} panel with new annual country-year data on six health and well-being outcomes: life expectancy, infant mortality, under-five mortality, premature non-communicable disease mortality, suicide mortality, and life satisfaction. The main explanatory variable is \emph{policy freedom}, capturing the economic freedom of monetary policy, trade policy and regulations. In annual two-way fixed-effects models for 2000--2023, higher policy freedom is associated with higher life expectancy, lower infant and under-five mortality, and higher life satisfaction, while the associations with premature NCD mortality and suicide mortality are weak. Results are stronger for non-OECD and non-democratic countries. The paper also shows that different types of economic freedom behave as substitutes rather than complements. Finally, a residualized country-contribution decomposition identifies the countries that drive the positive association and the counter-pattern cases that do not fit a simple economic-freedom-health narrative.

title: Measuring the Systemic Importance and Resilience of the Building Societies Sector

detail.title: Measuring the Systemic Importance and Resilience of the Building Societies Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research was funded by the Building Societies Association (BSA), which also provided data used in the study. The views expressed in the report are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the BSA.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Building Societies Association (BSA) through a Building Societies 250th Anniversary Award.

detail.abstract: This report provides a sector-wide assessment of the systemic importance and financial resilience of UK building societies. Using data on 67 building societies over 2000–2024, it combines conventional indicators of solvency with three complementary systemic-risk measures: Z-scores, a Leave-One-Out Z-score transformation, indirectly estimated SRISK based on balance-sheet fundamentals, and an asset-growth-based Exposure–ΔCoVaR framework. The results show that building societies are more highly capitalised and exhibit lower but more stable profitability than UK banks, resulting in consistently higher Z-scores and greater resilience during the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. Their inclusion increases aggregate financial-system solvency, indicating that the sector acts predominantly as a stabiliser rather than an amplifier of systemic stress. On average over 2000–2024, building societies account for approximately 3.5% of aggregate UK SRISK, rising to 4.6% in 2024, and around 6% when the comparison is restricted to banks and building societies. However, more than 92% of sector-level SRISK is concentrated among the five largest societies. Building societies are also less exposed to system-wide stress than banks, experiencing materially smaller contractions in asset growth during adverse conditions. The findings support the inclusion of non-listed institutions in systemic-risk monitoring while providing evidence in favour of proportionate regulation, with enhanced supervisory attention focused on the largest societies.

title: Job-Worker Balance and Polycentric Transit-Oriented Development

detail.title: Job-Worker Balance and Polycentric Transit-Oriented Development

declarations.funderStatement: I wish to thank the National Institute for Transportation and Communities (NITC) which supported this work under Dissertation Fellowship Grant 1440, as well as funding via several Student Scholar awards. I also send thanks to the United States Federal Highway Administration for their funding via the Dwight D. Eisenhower Transportation Fellowship Program for 2018 and 2023. I also wish to thank Dr. Kristina M. Currans, who provided generous advisory assistance with these grants through the application process. I also wish to thank Dr. Arthur C. Nelson for his expert advice and for providing access to data we collected under NITC research grants: NITC-UA-1253, NITC-RR-1103.

detail.abstract: The spatial distribution of resources in cities has a significant direct influence on how well both firms and households can access needed resources, which include not just raw materials, housing, food, and water, but also the need for firms to access a regional labor market and workers to access locations of employment. This dissertation aims to further the literature on theory and empirical evidence geared towards increasing access to employment across regions. A formalized theory of Job-Worker Balance (JWB) provides an accessibility-based variant of the jobs-housing balance ratio (JHB), a balanced count of housing and jobs within some zone, such as a county or city. The JWB evaluates the accessibility of workers to relevant employment within a distance from home that reduces the burden of commuting. That distance comprises an optimal zone within which “internal capture” of workers’ commutes may occur. That is, the origin and destination of work trips are captured within the zone, and the zone constitutes an optimized commuting context. Further, internal capture results in short and low-cost commutes. Two related theories are incorporated in the JWB theory. Advocates of transit-oriented development (TOD) assert that it can increase employment access and lower transport costs. The study considers the relative effectiveness of TOD at improving workers’ access to jobs, and the dynamics in firms’ access to their needed workforce. TODs are two things at once: nodes on a transportation network and also centers of land use concentration. They are inherently centers of economic and social activity that concentrate these societal functions at a higher rate of density and land use mix than found in their surroundings. Further, TOD is enhanced by polycentric development theory, which posits that it can enhance the workforce’s access to locations of employment across an entire region by providing more central places where access to local and regional linkages is highest. Quantitative spatial and temporal analysis using new methods and theories that add to the robustness of the research is applied to regions across the United States. The study also analyzes demographics, regional development patterns and urban form. Findings of the study indicate that the theoretical attributes of a JWB exist in various degrees of prominence and relevance across regions; they are not structurally uniform across all areas. It also finds that short commutes are not always associated with jobs-housing balance; there is a spatial non-stationarity to the association. This indicates a need to revise the jobs-housing balance. As expected, internal capture is generally positively associated with the jobs-labor balance ratio and income match in places of higher land use mix, centering and intensity that are connected to the regional transit network. Also, workers in higher wage classifications or in certain job sectors are found to enjoy higher rates of internal capture. Economic effects of segregation remain influential in redlined districts.

title: Open-Sourcing Patents, 1991-2026: Non-Assertion Pledges, Patent Clauses, Defensive Pools and Public-Health Licensing as Counter-Models to Financialisation

detail.title: Open-Sourcing Patents, 1991-2026: Non-Assertion Pledges, Patent Clauses, Defensive Pools and Public-Health Licensing as Counter-Models to Financialisation

keywords: technological commons JEL Codes: K11 (Property Law -Intellectual Property)

detail.abstract: This article documents, over the 1991-2026 period, the progressive emergence of a set of mechanisms that may be characterised as "open source of the patent" — unilateral non-assertion pledges, open licenses incorporating patent clauses, defensive pools and technological commons, and emergency public-health mechanisms — which constitute, in several respects, the counter-model to the financialisation examined in Article 5 of the series. Four balanced axes are analysed. First axis: unilateral non-assertion pledges, from IBM's Statement of Non-Assertion covering 500 patents dated January 11, 2005, through the Tesla pledge of June 12, 2014 ("All Our Patent Are Belong To You"), the Toyota open licenses on FCV patents (January 5, 2015, 5,680 patents) and then on hybrid and electric patents (April 3, 2019, approximately 24,000 patents), the Google Open Patent Non-Assertion Pledge of March 28, 2013, up to the recent Bluesky Patent Non-Aggression Pledge of October 1, 2025. Second axis: open licenses incorporating explicit patent clauses, from the Apache License 2.0 of January 2004 (Section 3), the GNU General Public License v3 of June 29, 2007 (Section 11, whose drafting was delayed by the Novell-Microsoft agreement of November 2, 2006), the Mozilla Public License 2.0 of January 3, 2012 (Section 2.3), and the Twitter Innovator's Patent Agreement (announced April 17, 2012, published in version 1.0 on May 21, 2013). Third axis: technological commons and defensive pools, from the Open Invention Network incorporated on October 31, 2005 (initial funding of USD 160 million, more than 4,000 members reached on February 18, 2025), through LOT Network (July 10, 2014, more than 6,300 members according to the 2025 report), Unified Patents (2012), the Allied Security Trust (January 1, 2007), the Defensive Patent License (Schultz-Urban, published November 16, 2013), up to the recent emergence of the Shared AI License Foundation (SAIL, announced in late 2025 by IBM, Meta, Microsoft, Anthropic and Genentech, formal press release April 2026). Fourth axis: emergency public-health mechanisms deployed in response to COVID-19, including the WHO Technology Access Pool (C-TAP, May 29, 2020), the Open COVID Pledge (April 7, 2020, approximately 500,000 patents), the Moderna pledge of October 8, 2020 partially withdrawn on March 7, 2022, and the MPP-Merck and MPP-Pfizer licenses of October-November 2021. The analysis identifies three cross-cutting lessons and formulates a research agenda for the 2026-2030 period.

reference: Volume 61.2 Harvard Civil Rights - Civil Liberties Law Review 615 (2026)
title: Systemic Racism as Negligence

detail.title: Systemic Racism as Negligence

publicationDetails.detailsText: Volume 61.2 Harvard Civil Rights - Civil Liberties Law Review 615 (2026)

detail.abstract:
Stark racial disparities persist across societal institutions. People of color face disproportionate policing, harsher sentencing, higher rates of unemployment, and unequal access to education and healthcare. These disparities are not solely the result of individual racial animus, but of institutional policies that ignore the enduring structures of racial power. Rather than addressing these systemic harms, the recent wave of anti-CRT legislation entrenches these racial realities further by codifying racial erasure into law.

This Article argues that systemic racism, defined as racial inequity produced by facially neutral policies that disregard the historical accumulation of racial power, constitutes a legally cognizable harm under existing negligence doctrine. Negligence law holds institutions liable when a breach of duty causes foreseeable harm, regardless of intent, as long as the elements of duty, breach, causation, and damages are met. Courts have recognized institutional negligence in the context of toxic tort, corporate malfeasance, and public health failures where diffuse injuries result from systemic practices or institutional design choices. While tort law has evolved to encompass institutional responsibility for systemic risk, courts have failed to apply this framework to racialized institutional harm. This failure reflects not a doctrinal incapacity, but a jurisprudential reluctance to move beyond intent-based antidiscrimination models that obscure structural racial injury.

Drawing on Critical Race Theory (CRT), this Article proposes a doctrinal recognition that treats systemic racism as a foreseeable institutional harm actionable under negligence while also critiquing the evidentiary and conceptual limitations of antidiscrimination law, particularly intent-based frameworks. Unlike antidiscrimination law, negligence does not require proof of intent and allows for liability where institutional actions or omissions create foreseeable risk. A detailed case study of Georgia’s Forsyth County Schools illustrates how the systemic racism as negligence framework would apply to anti-CRT policies that foreseeably reinforce racial subordination. Ultimately, this Article offers a doctrinal intervention: a systemic racism negligence framework grounded in tort law and informed by CRT, which provides a normatively urgent and legally viable pathway for redressing systemic racial harm.

title: The Relationship Between Corporate Governance and Firm Performance in Developing Countries: Empirical Evidence and Policy Frameworks
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Relationship Between Corporate Governance and Firm Performance in Developing Countries: Empirical Evidence and Policy Frameworks
detail.abstract: Corporate governance has emerged as a cornerstone of financial economics, corporate finance, and enterprise sustainability, particularly within emerging and developing economies. This paper investigates the empirical relationship between internal governance mechanisms specifically board independence, ownership concentration, financial disclosure quality, audit committee effectiveness, and executive compensation structures and operational performance metrics (ROA, ROE, and market valuation via Tobin's Q). Utilizing a multi-theoretical framework synthesizing Agency Theory, Stakeholder Theory, Stewardship Theory, and Resource Dependency Theory, we examine how institutional frictions, weak legal enforcement, political intervention, and agency costs condition corporate efficiency. Synthesizing quantitative modeling techniques with institutional empirical evidence, including comparative insights from corporate governance initiatives across Sub-Saharan Africa and Asia, this study outlines actionable econometric specifications and policy reforms essential for boosting market transparency, investor confidence, and macroeconomic capitalization.

title: An Integrated Optimization Model for Home Healthcare Routing and Scheduling with Synchronization, Break Scheduling, and Temporal Stability
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: An Integrated Optimization Model for Home Healthcare Routing and Scheduling with Synchronization, Break Scheduling, and Temporal Stability
detail.abstract: Home healthcare organizations must construct daily schedules that use constrained caregiver capacity efficiently while preserving continuity of care, predictable appointment times, household-level coordination, and compliance with working-time regulations. This paper develops an integrated optimization framework for the home healthcare routing and scheduling problem that incorporates synchronized visits, patient--caregiver preferences and previous-caregiver continuity, coordination of co-located patients, location-specific and location-flexible breaks, and appointment-time stability. The problem is solved on a daily basis, with historical information entering through two temporal references: the appointment time most recently communicated to the patient and the baseline routine established at the beginning of the care episode. This dual-horizon formulation distinguishes the cost of changing an announced schedule from the cost of drifting away from an established routine. We compare a mixed-integer linear formulation, a solver-native list-and-interval formulation (Hexaly), and two heuristic benchmarks. The computational study uses real operational data from a partner home healthcare organization, with limited controlled modification introduced to activate break and synchronization features not exercised in this particular partner's dataset. The results show that coverage depends not only on aggregate caregiver availability but also on the temporal, spatial, and qualification alignment of capacity with demand; on these instances, where requested workload plus estimated average travel typically exceeds contracted capacity, the model serves a share of demand comparable to the organization's own realized schedules, and increasing the priority on coverage does not close the shortfall. They further show that moderate changes in managerial priorities can substantially reduce the modeled penalties associated with caregiver continuity and appointment-time stability, with limited additional travel, waiting, and overtime.

title: Individual and interregional free-riding in coupled vaccination games: a three-level efficiency decomposition
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Individual and interregional free-riding in coupled vaccination games: a three-level efficiency decomposition
detail.abstract: Vaccination externalities operate at two distinct decision scales. Individuals do not internalize the protection they create within their population, while regional authorities may ignore protection exported to connected populations. Comparing voluntary vaccination directly with a centralized optimum conflates these mechanisms. We formulate a two-population pre-epidemic vaccination game with three decision levels: a nonatomic individual equilibrium, a Nash equilibrium between regional regulators, and a centralized social optimum. The epidemic outcome is determined by the exact multigroup SIR final-size relation. Row-stochastic reciprocal mixing matrices keep the system reproduction number fixed while epidemiological coupling and population size are varied. Implicit differentiation of the final-size relation identifies the cross-population marginal benefits omitted by regional decision makers. In a representative asymmetric-cost regime with $\Rzero=3$, voluntary individuals choose coverages $(1.000,0.000)$, regional regulators choose $(0.840,0.512)$, and the central planner chooses $(1.000,0.396)$. The corresponding costs are $0.4339$, $0.2931$, and $0.2618$. Thus, $81.8\%$ of the absolute individual-to-central gap arises within populations and $18.2\%$ arises between regional regulators; the pure interregional efficiency deficit is $10.7\%$. A 165-point joint scan shows that substantial losses require the interaction of epidemiological coupling and cost asymmetry and reach $13.9\%$ on the scanned domain. A separate seven-point series shows that the mechanism persists for $1.5\leq\Rzero\leq5$ and is strongest near $\Rzero=2$. Central coordination need not raise vaccination in every region: it reallocates effort toward locations where vaccination produces protection at lower cost. This distinction separates under-provision from misallocation and provides a reproducible benchmark for decentralized vaccination policy.

title: Rules for Changing the Rules: Strategic Reviews and the Maintenance of Monetary Regimes
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Rules for Changing the Rules: Strategic Reviews and the Maintenance of Monetary Regimes
detail.abstract: Credible monetary regimes face an adaptation paradox. They must change to remain effective, yet change can make their commitments look negotiable. The problem is newly urgent. Frameworks were tested first by persistent undershooting and the effective lower bound, then by the post-pandemic inflation surge, while central-bank instruments and responsibilities expanded. We study strategic reviews as institutions for governing adaptation without reopening the nominal anchor. A new documentary database covers 40 jurisdictions, 33 framework episodes, and 13 baseline reviews. None replaces the anchor wholesale. Reviews instead rework forecasting, communication, governance, instruments, and decision procedures. Review starts form an advanced-economy wave in 2017–24, but annual timing does not identify a diffusion chain. Strategic reviews are commitment-preserving maintenance—rules for changing the rules without renegotiating the anchor.

title: Strategic Control Rights: A Missing Dimension of Finance The State-contingent Allocation of Control over Economically Significant Assets

detail.title: Strategic Control Rights: A Missing Dimension of Finance The State-contingent Allocation of Control over Economically Significant Assets
detail.abstract: Finance has a sophisticated account of who owns an asset and a thinner one of who controls it — or rather, it has theorised control almost entirely as an attribute of ownership. The property-rights theory of the firm equates control with the ownership of residual rights, and the regulatory apparatus has followed, building investment screening, beneficial-ownership transparency, and state-owned-enterprise governance around the question of who holds title. This paper argues that ownership is an unreliable proxy for control over economically significant assets, because a distinct and largely unmapped class of contractual entitlements — security interests, step-in and replacement rights, negative covenants, cross-default and enforcement provisions, exclusive offtake and exit rights — allocates control contingently, vesting it in parties who own nothing just when assets come under stress. The paper names these Strategic Control Rights and makes three moves: it defines them and separates them from ownership, from shareholder voting, and from conventional creditor rights conceived as purely pecuniary; it identifies their defining feature as state-contingency, control resting with the owner in normal conditions and migrating to the rights-holder at distress, default, and enforcement, the moments when control matters most; and it argues that where the underlying asset is strategically significant, these private reallocations carry consequences that ownership-centred regulation cannot see. Strategic Control Rights builds on the incomplete-contracts account of financial contracting. Those models showed that the efficient financial contract makes control state-contingent: the entrepreneur keeps control in good states, and the investor takes it in bad ones. This paper does not rest there. It converts that result into a positive framework: it names the instruments through which control migrates, unifies them across the doctrinal silos in which they are studied, drops the analysis to the level of the specific asset, and carries the question from the private efficiency the models asked about to the distributive and public consequences they did not. The result is conceptual infrastructure — a vocabulary and analytic for control without ownership — on which application-specific work spanning project finance, supply chains, sovereign risk, and national security can be built. The dimension is one and the theory is general.

title: The Role of Lifelong and Self-directed Learning in Creative and Business Industries
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Role of Lifelong and Self-directed Learning in Creative and Business Industries
detail.abstract: In modern industries, adaptation and skill development are essential, and lifelong and selfdirected learning are becoming key abilities for long-term career success. The purpose of this study was to examine the effect of self-directed learning practices on leadership development, critical thinking skills, and problem-solving skills of professionals in the creative and business industry. The study was based on the concept of heutagogical learning, as well as well-known self-directed learning theories, and a comprehensive instrument with Likert-scale assessments and reflective open-ended questions were used to survey 7 early to mid-career professionals (57% creative sector, 43% business sector). The results showed that self-directed learning engagement was found to be strongly positively correlated with the level of leadership confidence, with the average leadership growth score of the participants being 3.5/5 or 70%. It is observed that creative individuals showed greater intrinsic motivation and curiosity-oriented learning, while the business sector was more oriented towards results. Skill development in Critical thinking and Problem solving had moderate growth (74% aggregate), but there were some inconsistencies in the use of these skills in day-today work activities. There were significant barriers such as time restrictions, information overload, and motivational variations that were found to be obstacles to regular SLL practices. The study successfully validates the Dynamic Creative Professional persona framework and the mixed-methods survey design, which is effective in capturing the complexities of self-directed learning in the context of work.

title: Financial Statement Information Utilization and SMEs Profitability: Evidence from Selected Commercial Cities in Anambra State, Nigeria
affiliations: Institute of Management and Technology (IMT), Enugu

detail.title: Financial Statement Information Utilization and SMEs Profitability: Evidence from Selected Commercial Cities in Anambra State, Nigeria

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced the study
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved the collection of primary data through structured questionnaires conducted with participants who were fully informed about the purpose of the research. Participation was voluntary, and informed consent was obtained from all respondents prior to their involvement. Confidentiality and anonymity of all participants were strictly maintained throughout the study.
declarations.funderStatement: Self

detail.abstract: The ability of a business to manage its cash and use financial data is still essential to its survival and profitability, especially for SMEs in the industrial sectors of emerging nations. This study examined the effect of financial statement information utilization on the profitability of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in selected commercial cities of Anambra State, Nigeria The study's specific objectives were to examine the effect of income statement information utilization, changes in equity information utilization, and cash flow statement information utilization on the profitability of SMEs in selected commercial cities of Anambra State, Nigeria. A descriptive survey research approach was employed for the study while PESTEL assessment was employed to ensure a robust analysis. Taro Yamane (1967) statistical formula was used to determine a sample size of 301 respondents from a population of 1,217 SMEs operating within Awka, Nnewi and Onitsha Metropolis. Descriptive analysis and inferential analysis was conducted using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) Version 25. The study found that income statement information utilization, changes in equity information utilization, and cash flow statement information utilization has no significant influence on SMEs' profitability with p-values 0.596, 0.424 and 0.706 respectively. It is concluded that financial information practices utilization among SMEs in Awka, Nnewi and Onitsha Metropolis do not significantly influence their profitability. It recommends SMEs examine their financial inflows, outflows, and equity changes on a regular basis to ensure better financial control and greater profitability.

title: Forward Belief Volatility in Prediction Markets: A Budget-Anchored Term Structure

detail.title: Forward Belief Volatility in Prediction Markets: A Budget-Anchored Term Structure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Belief Systems (True Craft Ventures LLC), which intends to publish indices based on the methodology described in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Prediction markets report what the market believes about an event, but not how much that belief is expected to move. Trailing realized volatility is backward-looking, while event contracts generally lack the derivative markets used to construct conventional implied volatility. This paper develops Forward Belief Volatility (FBV), a budget-anchored term structure of expected probability movement. For a binary contract whose forward-normalized price 𝑝 is a martingale under a pricing measure, expected remaining quadratic variation is exactly 𝑝(1-𝑝), model-free and including jumps. The current price therefore identifies total variance to resolution, but not its allocation across calendar time. FBV represents that allocation with an information clock. Date ladders provide pricing-measure occurrence timing at their quoted dates. Bracket and combination markets provide terminal structure but not its timing. Resolved-contract histories provide physical-measure timing forecasts. Each output is labeled accordingly, separating price-implied components from estimated ones. FBV is reported as root-mean-square probability movement over standard forward horizons, together with the exact binary to-resolution total and the share of the variance budget assigned to each horizon. A worked illustration using 2026 U.S. midterm markets demonstrates the construction, and a prospective validation protocol tests whether richer inputs add information beyond price and calendar. Because its calendar allocation is generally estimated rather than traded, FBV is a budget-anchored forecast rather than a conventional implied-volatility measure.

title: Structural Bombing: When the Analysis of a Subordinate Becomes a Mirror for the Supervisor
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Structural Bombing: When the Analysis of a Subordinate Becomes a Mirror for the Supervisor
detail.abstract:
This study examines how two structural analysis documents altered their functions as they moved through an organizational hierarchy. The first document, termed “Structural Bombing,” was created to analyze a lower-level employee whose recurring behavior included rigid adherence to personal methods, immediate rejection of alternative views, anger in response to unexpected changes, hostile attribution, externalization of blame, and deterioration of collaborative relationships. The document was initially submitted to the employee’s supervisor as a managerial report. After its submission, the employee left the workplace, while the supervisor’s own expressions of anger temporarily decreased. Although causality cannot be established, this temporal sequence suggests that an analysis directed at a subordinate may also operate as an indirect mirror for the supervisor.

The behavioral change did not persist. When anger-based public correction reappeared, the employee who raised the concern argued that the issue could no longer be treated simply as a lack of awareness or opportunity for reflection. Instead, the recurrence indicated the limits of relying on voluntary self-correction and supported organizational interventions such as supervisory oversight, third-party dialogue, anger-management training, and adjustment of managerial authority. Following direct structural feedback and a request for involvement by higher management, communication with the person raising the concern was reduced through nonresponse, exclusion from shared channels, and avoidance of contact. A second document, termed “Serial Structural Bombing,” was then created to analyze the supervisor’s managerial behavior and the subsequent withdrawal from feedback.

When the two documents were submitted together to higher-level managers and the headquarters human resources department, the first document changed from a report about a subordinate into a comparative standard for evaluating the supervisor. This study conceptualizes that transformation as document function reversal and identifies three related mechanisms: the indirect mirror effect, hierarchical reflection asymmetry, and the Structural Bombing Cycle Model. The findings suggest that organizational documents are not passive records. They can shape behavior, preserve voice after interpersonal communication has collapsed, move problems across hierarchical boundaries, and convert individual incidents into institutional questions. Whether structural analysis contributes to organizational learning depends not only on the accuracy of the analysis, but also on whether the organization can examine the reflected structure without silencing the person who raised it.

title: Connected Technology as a Solution (CTaaS)

detail.title: Connected Technology as a Solution (CTaaS)
detail.abstract:
Connected Technology — the phones, tablets, laptops, routers, and sensors that businesses, agencies, and non-profits run on — is sold as pieces, not solutions. Hardware, software, and connectivity come from separate vendors, under separate contracts, with no single party accountable for the combined result. This paper presents Connected Technology as a Solution (CTaaS), a managed-technology category built around a documented six-stage methodology, the 6S Framework: Sourcing, Stocking, Synchronization, Supply, Support, and Sustainability.

The paper first shows why the two closest existing categories, Managed IT services and Device as a Service, each solve only part of the problem, and argues that CTaaS is not a better version of either but a structurally distinct category: it carries no minimum device count, no fixed device-type list, no ceiling on scale, and a stage-gated, audit-ready operating architecture that neither predecessor category possesses. It develops a central and underexplored insight, that CTaaS aggregates in two directions at once, consolidating a customer's fragmented technology into one window while pooling many customers' demand into real buying power. The paper in Appendix C translates the story of CTaaS in infographics to narrate CTaaS and its applications in Visuals.

The paper presents a physical blueprint for a CTaaS facility, a governance and workforce architecture built on 108 stage-gated operating steps, and verified evidence from a family of published field applications spanning home health care, non-profit digital inclusion, small-business transportation and logistics, and rural connectivity. It gives particular attention to the paper's central claim of national significance: that a CTaaS provider's remote, single-window reach is national from the day its first facility opens, and that onsite presence then thickens organically outward from a regional starting point without ever limiting the provider's reach to that region. A worked regional-launch case, drawn from a real, publicly documented CTaaS venture beginning in a single Opportunity Zone community, is used to demonstrate this mechanism concretely. The paper closes with market sizing across every segment CTaaS now touches, and a discussion of sustainability, workforce, and cybersecurity implications for the national economy.

title: Beyond the Initial Filing: Cybersecurity Incident Disclosure Chains Under Sec Form 8-K Item 1.05

detail.title: Beyond the Initial Filing: Cybersecurity Incident Disclosure Chains Under Sec Form 8-K Item 1.05

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available corporate filings and does not involve human participants, patient data, interviews, experiments, or personally identifiable research data.

detail.abstract: SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 requires public companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents, often before the nature, scope, or impact of an incident is fully determined. Yet empirical research commonly treats each filing as a standalone event. We examine how cybersecurity incident disclosure evolves after the initial filing by reconstructing 53 disclosure chains from 78 Item 1.05 records filed between December 2023 and July 2026. Review of the full filing text and EDGAR histories identifies six chains that first entered the public record through Item 8.01 or Item 7.01, yielding a common-entry primary sample of 47 Item 1.05-origin chains. Nineteen chains received a subsequent Item 1.05 filing. Among these updated chains, the median time to the first update was 21 days, and eight changed the incident classification recorded in the frozen source. Survival models estimate a lower update hazard after the SEC staff clarification of May 21, 2024, but the association is imprecise and cannot be uniquely attributed to that date after accounting for calendar trends, alternative breakpoints, common follow-up, and chain-level resampling. The evidence therefore supports a broad temporal decline in observed update propensity rather than a discrete regulatory effect. The paper's principal contribution is methodological and regulatory: filing-level designs can misidentify event dates, treat updates as independent incidents, and backfill initial information with facts disclosed only later. A chain-preserving architecture separates first public disclosure, materiality determination, and subsequent amendments, improving measurement for studies of market reactions, disclosure quality, and cyber-risk governance.

title: Benchmarking Economic Performance after the Commodity Supercycle: Evidence from Pacific Basin Mining Economies
affiliations: Universidad de Las Américas, Chile

detail.title: Benchmarking Economic Performance after the Commodity Supercycle: Evidence from Pacific Basin Mining Economies
detail.abstract: The end of the commodity supercycle driven by Chinese demand generated a widespread growth slowdown across Pacific Basin mineral-exporting economies. However, to date, no agreed benchmark exists for determining whether this reflects exceptional country underperformance or the common adjustment to a shared external shock. This article argues that the diagnosis depends critically on how the benchmark is constructed. It proposes a practical framework that combines three complementary approaches: a structural benchmark based on predetermined fundamentals and period effects, a benchmark based on mining peers exposed to similar external conditions, and a synthetic control used as a diagnostic of benchmark fragility rather than as an independent estimate of performance. The framework is illustrated using three Pacific Basin mining economies, Chile, Peru and Australia, which represent contrasting post-supercycle trajectories. For Chile, the structural exercise identifies a moderate shortfall of 0.4-0.6 percentage points of annual GDP per capita growth relative to expected performance, whereas the mining-peer counterpart places Chile close to, or slightly above, comparable economies. The synthetic control proves highly sensitive to donor-pool composition and fails the invariance criterion proposed here, illustrating the importance of evaluating benchmark robustness before drawing substantive conclusions. Applying the same methodology to Peru and Australia yields clearly different diagnoses, supporting the framework's discriminant validity. The results suggest that much of the post-2014 slowdown among Pacific Basin mining economies reflects common adjustment to the end of the commodity supercycle, and that assessments of relative economic performance are more credible when based on triangulation across complementary benchmarks rather than on a single counterfactual.

detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence is being coupled to effectors whose actions do not undo, at machine timescales no human reaction can match. The prevailing responses govern the model: they train dispositions, evaluate behavior, and regulate providers, and all of them leave the actuation boundary, the point where a proposal becomes an irreversible act, without an independent, physical, temporally adequate control. This paper specifies that control. We fix the harnessed system, a model coupled to scaffolding and effectors, as the risk object, and show that the decisive risk condition is a property of deployment topology, decidable today without any forecast of machine capability. On that trajectory-agnostic footing, we construct the framework in four layers: a three-dimensional governance space of authority, constraint, and provenance; a dual-engine architecture that realizes its boundary, with a verification protocol proved to terminate safely; a human-cognitive layer that closes the failure classes no gate can reach-omission, over-alignment, and silent degradation; and a provenance layer that makes every verified action an unforgeable, meterable record. The framework is validated three ways: as the missing controller under a systems-theoretic accident model, as the invariant conclusion of premise sets that cannot all be true, and against a staged falsification program with named refuting results. The paper closes with a requirement-level normative core of twenty-four clauses across three standards, and a decision rule, the closing window, that replaces forecast countdowns with two measurable clocks.

The author serves on the editorial boards of the Journal of Health Organization and Management (Emerald) and Public Administration Quarterly (SAGE), and is a director of a different Japanese academic society. None of these roles bears on this study.

detail.abstract: Professional and academic societies in health services research and health care management draw their members from two populations, academics and practitioners, and their governing organs decide what the field asks. How the balance between those populations is distributed across the layers of a society’s governance has not been described, in large part because societies are under no obligation to retain their past rosters. This study reconstructs three consecutive terms of the councillor layer, the board and the presidency of an incorporated Japanese society in this field from captures held in a public web archive, coding each office-holder as university-affiliated or not from the affiliation the society published at the time of service. The proportion of university affiliations falls as the layers rise, from 87.3 and 77.8 per cent among councillors to 57.1, 53.8 and 50.0 per cent on the board, while the presidency is university-affiliated throughout. The mixture on the board is not drawn from the electing layer: every director who reached the board without holding a councillor seat did so through a nomination power created by amendment in 2022, and every such director held a non-university affiliation. Because the councillors, and not the board, are the legal members of the association, the layer that registers as balanced is not the layer that holds the vote. A single index for a single body is a poor description of an organisation’s governance.

(2011, 2012), deriving the discrete and continuous expressions for the Funding Cost Adjustment (FCA) and the Funding Benefit Adjustment (FBA).
