detail.title: Three Ways to Close a Model: On the Logical Justification for Solution Concepts in Economics
detail.abstract: The philosophy of economics has developed rich accounts of what models are-isolations, credible worlds, fables, mediating instruments-while saying little about the device that converts a model's structure into claims: the solution concept. We argue that solution concepts constitute a distinct locus of methodological commitment-separable from, though interacting with, the realism of assumptionsand that economics operates at least three families of them whose justificatory logics differ in kind: Walrasian closure, licensed by limit theorems and engineered institutions while its textbook dynamics fail in general; strategic closure, whose epistemic and refinement audits revealed demanding conditions and ineliminable plurality; and dynamical closure-steady states and balanced growth paths-licensed calibrationally against stylized facts. Received interpretations of solution concepts as predictions, norms, or self-enforcing agreements fail to generalize across the families. We defend a functionalist alternative: solution concepts are material inference rules-Rylean tickets-vindicated through distinct feedback channels, including a performative channel-building a ticket's own conditions of application-that economics has institutionalized as no other science has. Model appraisal is therefore two-dimensional, extending to closure the credibility questions hitherto asked only of structure. A comparative check against evolutionary biology and ecology shows most of this situation to be scientifically ordinary; only reflexivity institutionalized as a vindication channel is economics' own. We close by observing that the standard curriculum presents the three logics as one continuous method, in inverse order of their epistemic audit.

title: Trading Off Openness: Economic Information and Immigration Policy Preferences
affiliations: CMCC - Centro Euro-Mediterraneo sui Cambiamenti Climatici, Università degli Studi di Milano, University of Bologna and

detail.title: Trading Off Openness: Economic Information and Immigration Policy Preferences
detail.abstract: We conducted a survey experiment with over 8,000 participants in Germany, Hungary and Italy to examine how information about the economic impact of immigration affects the support for more open immigration policies. Respondents who received projections showing higher future incomes under more open immigration policies reported greater support for these policies. The treatment also partly changed how prior attitudes affected policy preferences. Structural estimates suggest that majority support for immigration above current levels would require annual per-capita income gains of about 1.2% in Italy and 1.7% in Germany, and still larger or unattainable gains in Hungary. These increases are large relative to recent historical growth rates, suggesting that economic benefits alone are unlikely to generate vast support for more open immigration policies.

title: What are the Bottlenecks to Secure Strongly Bonded Teamwork Spirit in Ethiopia's Federal Level Public Institutions? (An Ordered Probit Model)

detail.title: What are the Bottlenecks to Secure Strongly Bonded Teamwork Spirit in Ethiopia's Federal Level Public Institutions? (An Ordered Probit Model)
detail.abstract: Team enables people to cooperate, enhance individual skills and provide constructive feedback without any conflict between individuals (Jones, et.al 2007). This study conducted to explore the factors that affect the culture of team works in federal level ministry offices in Ethiopia and to suggest the mechanisms to overcome those challenges and utilize the good opportunities. In the study the mixed methods of research design have been employed. The study used both primary and secondary data. The primary data has been collected by using questionnaire, focus group discussion and in-depth interview from the members of change army. Secondary data have been collected from different published and unpublished documents. The sample sizes in the study were 322 respondents. The data has been analyzed through ordered probit model with the help of STATA software. The finding of the study showed that almost all identified individual, structural, institutional and managerial challenges, had statistically significant impact for breaking the culture of team work except for Lack of active participation in all three models, Absence of group thinking in second and third model and inappropriate group size, Lack of visionary change army leader, unfair duty and responsibility sharing, Political Interference and lack of decision making skills in third model. Since, more than ninety percent of identified variables had statistically significant impact in terms of breaking down the culture of teamwork in Ethiopia, government and all decision makers in the country should have to work to minimize these identified challenges.

title: Creditors’ Seniority and Sovereign Risk: Evidence from Debt Composition
affiliations: Université d'Auvergne - Clermont 1 - Centre d'Etudes et de Recherches sur le Developpement International (CERDI), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Creditors’ Seniority and Sovereign Risk: Evidence from Debt Composition
detail.abstract: We provide new evidence on the de facto seniority structure of sovereign debt. Using a measure of the Relative Percentage in Default (RPID) by creditor group for 119 low-income and emerging market countries over the period 1980–2022, we show that debt owed to the IMF and the World Bank is, on average, the most senior, followed by debt owed to official bilateral creditors. Private creditors, notably bondholders and commercial banks, are on average junior to official creditors, with commercial banks being the least prioritized group for repayments. Beyond characterizing the seniority hierarchy, our empirical analysis shows that creditor composition has economically meaningful implications for sovereign risk. Using an instrumental variable estimation, we show that IMF credit outstanding as a share of GNI is robustly and negatively associated with the probability of a debt crisis. This stabilizing effect weakens progressively as debt stocks rise, suggesting that the IMF's crisis-preventing role diminishes in situations of severe debt overhang. Turning to sovereign borrowing costs, we find that IMF lending is negatively associated with sovereign bond spreads.

title: Trade-related Vulnerabilities and the Controversial Boundaries of Member States’ Economic Security in the EU
affiliations: University of Trento - Department of Economics and Management and University of Trento - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Trade-related Vulnerabilities and the Controversial Boundaries of Member States’ Economic Security in the EU
detail.abstract: Growing geopolitical tensions have renewed interest in trade-related vulnerabilities as a component of economic security. However, the lack of a well-defined conceptual framework around the concept of economic security implies the co-existence of different definitions, shifting boundaries and fuzzy policy prescriptions. Recent empirical work has developed product-level indicators of external dependence, typically combining information on import concentration, global supply concentration, and domestic substitutability. These methodologies are generally designed either for sovereign States or for the European Union treated as a single integrated area. This paper argues that they cannot be directly replicated to assess vulnerabilities at the level of individual EU Member States. The paper's methodological contribution shows that the EU's quasi-federal nature creates specific conceptual and measurement problems for Member State assessments, especially concerning the treatment of intra-EU sourcing in the construction of concentration and substitutability indicators. These choices affect the internal coherence of vulnerability metrics and reflect prior judgments about whether the relevant threat is economic coercion, broader supply disruption, or both. An empirical section applies one of the existing methodologies to highly disaggregated trade data to illustrate the impact of alternative treatments of intra-EU trade and compare different results.

title: Financial Returns Assumed Unlinked to Demand (FRAUD): Returns to Productive Investment Under Demand Exclusion

detail.title: Financial Returns Assumed Unlinked to Demand (FRAUD): Returns to Productive Investment Under Demand Exclusion
detail.abstract: This paper identifies Financial Returns Assumed Unlinked to Demand (FRAUD), the mistaken inference that a model incorporating aggregate demand, investment, profits, and financial returns has thereby incorporated expected aggregate demand into the expected return governing additional productive capacity. It distinguishes representational demand inclusion from expected-return demand inclusion and shows that the latter requires expected demand to enter the complete return-forming system, directly or indirectly through expected sales, utilization, prices, markups, cash flow, default risk, financing conditions, or other return determinants. The paper compares two otherwise similar investment architectures. In the demand-excluded architecture, expected demand affects current activity but not the expected productive return, so autonomous demand does not alter investment or steady-state capital through that channel. In the demand-responsive architecture, stronger expected demand raises anticipated utilization or sales, increases the expected return on additional capacity, and raises investment and steady-state capital when this effect exceeds any required-return response. The analysis distinguishes structural exclusion from zero net effects generated by offsetting mechanisms, temporary demand, excess capacity, or adjustment frictions. The resulting diagnostic clarifies when investment models genuinely incorporate expected demand and prevents the presence of demand elsewhere from being mistaken for demand inclusion in productive-return formation.

title: Whose Interest Does the Digital Euro’s Holding Limits Serve?

detail.title: Whose Interest Does the Digital Euro’s Holding Limits Serve?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No individual participants or case studies relating to individuals are covered by this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was provided.

detail.abstract: The European Central Bank’s proposed holding limit on the digital euro — commonly cited at around €3,000 for individuals and zero for businesses — is justified as a safeguard against destabilizing deposit flight from commercial banks during a financial crisis. This paper examines that justification against the ECB’s own simulation results and against recent theoretical work on the neutrality of substituting public for private money, and finds the stability rationale considerably weaker than commonly assumed. Drawing on CEPR’s 2026 Digital Money report, it shows that central bank pass-through funding to banks can, under identifiable conditions, leave bank lending capacity largely unaffected by digital-euro adoption, and that the quantity-based limit chosen instead functions more effectively as a defense of existing bank deposit franchises than as a financial stability instrument. The paper argues that the holding-limit debate is best understood as a proxy fight over a larger question: as the ECB takes on a larger operational role in bank funding to accommodate the digital euro — expanding its balance sheet somewhat if it chooses to fully offset the resulting deposit outflows — then who should set the criteria by which the resulting collateral framework allocates credit across the economy? It concludes that this question deserves to be settled openly, through democratic input, rather than by default through a technical parameter.

title: Optimal Policy Reforms
affiliations: Tulane University, Tulane University and Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro

detail.title: Optimal Policy Reforms
detail.abstract: This paper develops a general framework to construct optimal policy reforms allowing for fiscal spillovers onto other policymakers. The optimal reform direction depends on a single sufficient statistic for each policy, the welfare per internal cost (WPIC), which measures the welfare gain per dollar spent by the policymaker accounting for the welfare impacts of fiscal spillovers onto other policymakers. The WPIC collapses to the (welfare-weighted) marginal-value-of-public-funds if there are no fiscal spillovers and to the (welfare-weighted) net-social-benefit-per-dollar if behavioral costs accrue externally. We provide numerical examples illustrating that fiscal spillovers can meaningfully change the optimal reform direction.

title: A Priori Power Analysis Wizard: A Guided Interface for Choosing and Justifying Sample-Size Calculations in Behavioral Science

detail.title: A Priori Power Analysis Wizard: A Guided Interface for Choosing and Justifying Sample-Size Calculations in Behavioral Science

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this work because it describes the development of a software tool and does not involve human participants, human data, animal subjects, or biological materials.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Power analysis is often presented as a calculation. In practice, the hardest choices come first: deciding which analysis matches the design and explaining why a particular effect size deserves to drive the sample-size target. Popular tools such as G*Power and the pwr R package assume that both decisions have already been made. The A Priori Power Analysis Wizard brings them into the workflow. Its plain-language guide connects a research design to one of sixteen analysis families, while a separate effect-size step asks users to choose among established conventions, a conservative estimate from previous evidence, or a smallest effect worth detecting. The browser-based application then produces the required sample size together with paste-ready text that records the reasoning behind it. The software is open source, runs without installation or a remote server, and is designed for teaching as well as research planning. The paper also develops two broader lessons. First, it shows in simple terms why planning from a barely significant published result can leave a new study with only about one third of the sample it needs once uncertainty in that result is taken seriously. Second, it shows why matching a set of benchmark answers is not enough to validate statistical software: property-based tests uncovered failures that hundreds of conventional tests had missed. Together, the tool and its validation framework make power analysis easier to explain, reproduce, inspect, and challenge.

title: Degrees of Mobility: Shifting Low-Income Students to Higher Quality Colleges
affiliations: , Harvard University, National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Gerald R. Ford School of Public Policy, University of Michigan at Ann Arbor, Columbia University, University of Michigan at Ann Arbor, Colby College,  and Harvard University

detail.title: Degrees of Mobility: Shifting Low-Income Students to Higher Quality Colleges
detail.abstract: Earnings inequality among college graduates has grown, and returns to a bachelor's degree (BA) vary substantially across colleges. We experimentally evaluate a program that shifted high-achieving, low-income students into higher-quality colleges. Students randomly offered a guarantee of four years of tuition and fees at the University of Michigan were 21 percentage points more likely to enroll at a UM campus. The offer shifted students across colleges rather than into college: most compliers would otherwise have attended less-selective four-year colleges. HAIL increased four-year BA completion by 4 percentage points, but had no effect on attainment after six years. It substantially increased degree quality: students offered the scholarship were 12 percentage points more likely to earn a bachelor's degree from a highly or most selective college. IV estimates indicate that students induced to attend a University of Michigan campus were 56 percentage points more likely to earn such a degree. The increase in college quality predicts earnings gains of 18 to 25 percent. Faster degree completion adds about another 1 percent to the present discounted value of lifetime earnings.

title: Do Capital Flow Management Measures Respond to Geopolitical Risk? Evidence from Advanced and Emerging Market Economies
affiliations: University of Glasgow - Adam Smith Business School, International Monetary Fund (IMF),  and Bank for International Settlements (BIS)

detail.title: Do Capital Flow Management Measures Respond to Geopolitical Risk? Evidence from Advanced and Emerging Market Economies
detail.abstract: We examine whether geopolitical risk (GPR) shapes the use of capital flow management measures (CFMs). We combine a quarterly database of CFMs taken by advanced economies (AEs) and emerging market economies (EMEs) over 2000Q1-2019Q4 with country-specific GPR indices. We instrument domestic GPR with a foreign-GPR exposure measure based on bilateral geographic proximity. We find that a rise in GPR significantly increases the use of CFMs by EMEs, especially CFMs targeting outflows. By contrast, the estimated responses for AEs are statistically indistinguishable from zero. Within EMEs, outflow tightening is concentrated in countries with limited fiscal space, high external vulnerability, low reserve adequacy, explicit exchange-rate-management commitments, and high UIP deviations. Overall, the results are consistent with defensive outflow management: when GPR rises, vulnerable EMEs use CFMs to limit balance-sheet and external-financing pressures.

title: "Regulatory Contract Law and Employment-At-Will"
affiliations: University of Florida Levin College of Law

detail.title: "Regulatory Contract Law and Employment-At-Will"
detail.abstract: This chapter explores how regulatory contract theory might inform and reshape American employment law, in particular its distinct employment at-will doctrine that permits termination without cause. That principle, and its freedom-of-contract ethos, has long constrained and distorted efforts to regulate employment contracts. Substantive statutory intervention has been piecemeal and reactive. Labor laws that might have supported a collective contract model of regulation have been too weak to sustain a culture of union affiliation or successful bargaining. And individual employment contract law has developed in ways that enhance managerial power and stymie application of traditional policing doctrines. Accepting the futility of efforts to defeat employment-at-will, the chapter imagines how regulatory contract theory might blunt its edges. It advances a common law reform agenda that preserves the core of employment-at-will – employers' substantive discretion to terminate – but imposes non-waivable procedural and relational obligations, including reasonable notice of termination and good-faith limitations on changes to employment terms. The chapter concludes that a reorientation of employment-at-will doctrine, grounded in regulatory contract theory, can enhance workplace fairness while still preserving the basic structure of American employment law.

title: Competitive Effects of Digital Information Sharing: Insights from Retail Gasoline
affiliations: University of Melbourne, University of Liverpool, Clemson University - John E. Walker Department of Economics, Duke University - Fuqua School of Business, Economics Group and University of Melbourne

detail.title: Competitive Effects of Digital Information Sharing: Insights from Retail Gasoline
detail.abstract: Studies from retail gasoline markets worldwide have produced a wealth of evidence from a variety of contexts on the competitive effects of firms using digital platforms to share price or quantity information. We overview this body of research and discuss lessons for antitrust enforcement in detecting and remedying anticompetitive effects of digital information sharing.

title: Devroye's Jacobi and Pólya Samplers, Thorin Measures, and the Zeros of Ξ
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Devroye's Jacobi and Pólya Samplers, Thorin Measures, and the Zeros of Ξ
detail.abstract: The exact random variate generators of Devroye (2009) for the Jacobi laws J and J * , and the Pólya characteristic function method of Devroye (1984a), are statements about generalized gamma convolutions (GGC) and their Thorin measures. We develop the dictionary and then apply it to the Riemann Ξ function. Four points. (1) J, J * and the Pólya-Gamma family are GGCs whose Thorin measure is a counting measure on the squared zeros of cosh and sinh; the companion law J ′ is infinitely divisible but is not a GGC, its representing measure being signed. (2) The two rejection envelopes that make Devroye's algorithm almost rejection free are the two ends of the Thorin measure: the right envelope rate is min supp U , and the left envelope is the stable law whose index matches the Weyl growth of U. This recovers his constants π 2 /8 and exp{-1/(2x)} exactly, and it is a general recipe. (3) The series method is a certified sign oracle: Leibniz bracketing of an alternating series gives a computable two sided enclosure, which is the natural instrument for positivity claims about mixing and Thorin measures. (4) Applied to the incomplete gamma continuation of ξ used in Polson (2021a), the bounded mixing density of that paper yields an explicit Laplace dominating curve and hence an exact sampler for the Riemann-Pólya law, but exact simulation cannot certify the location of the zeros. We give the obstruction in two forms: a structural one, mixture representations deliver infinite divisibility while only convolution representations deliver real zeros, and a quantitative one, unbiased Monte Carlo estimation of Ξ(t) needs of order e πt/2 draws. What simulation can do is detect off line zeros through the oscillation frequency of a failed complete monotonicity test. All claims are checked numerically: the envelope ratio, the tail constants, the partial fraction coefficients, the positivity scan of that paper (whose minimum we identify in closed form as 2/(3N 2), a boundary effect rather than a near violation), and the Monte Carlo cost. Two technical points in the source paper are flagged for checking.

title: Prediction Markets, Bayes and Kalshi
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Prediction Markets, Bayes and Kalshi
detail.abstract: An event contract settles at one dollar or zero, so its price is a probability and the exchange is a market quoted in the currency of Bayes. We give a Bayesian account of trading such contracts, with the CFTC regulated exchange Kalshi as the leading case. Three ingredients are needed. First, a model whose latent parameter is low dimensional relative to the number of listed contracts, so that a few liquid quotes identify the whole board. Second, a posterior that carries parameter uncertainty into every derived contract rather than a plug in estimate. Third, a sizing rule. We show that Kelly betting on an exclusive family of contracts has an explicit water filling solution with a shadow price b that is strictly below one, so that contracts with negative naive expected value can enter the growth optimal portfolio as hedges, and that the optimal growth rate is i∈S p i log(p i /c i) + (1-p S) log b, which collapses to the Kullback-Leibler divergence KL(p∥c) when the book is fair. The Harville (1973) formula is treated as the canonical low dimensional generator of a combinatorially large contract set, with a Jensen argument showing that plug in exacta prices are biased downward. We recall the Skellam calibration of real time soccer odds of Feng et al. (2016) and the model free martingale diagnostics of Aldous (2013), whose halftime price and serious candidates principles give tests of a Kalshi board that require no model at all. Kalshi's fee θπ(1-π) with θ = 0.07 creates a no trade band of width 2θπ(1-π), at most 3.5 cents at the mid, and it changes which positions exist and not merely their size. An ϵ contamination prior that shrinks the posterior toward the price scales the Kelly stake by exactly 1-ϵ, which makes fractional Kelly a Bayes rule rather than a heuristic, and a simulation study shows that the shrinkage is worth roughly six times its cost once the trader's input is noisy rather than merely uncertain. For the maker side we derive the adverse selection spread on a binary contract, which is 4µp(1-p) for an informed order flow fraction µ and therefore has the same quadratic shape as the exchange fee, and we show that a log utility maker's inventory adjusted reservation price is p i /(ΛW i), falling directly out of the same first order conditions. Three real episodes anchor the framework: the 2025 federal shutdown duration ladder, whose twelve rungs are reproduced to within a cent by a one parameter hazard; the 2024 election board and its cross venue incoherence; and the favourite longshot bias documented on Kalshi by Bürgi et al. (2025), under which contracts below ten cents lose more than sixty percent of the money staked.

title: Exact Simulation for Bayesian Monte Carlo
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Exact Simulation for Bayesian Monte Carlo
detail.abstract: Bayesian computation is usually presented as a story about Markov chains. This paper argues that a large part of the practical gain comes instead from the older theory of non-uniform random variate generation, and then uses that theory to settle five problems it leaves open. Part I isolates four classical ideas, due to Devroye (1986), Hammersley and Handscomb (1964) and Ripley (1987), and follows each into a named Bayesian algorithm: von Neumann's series method, the ratio of uniforms, exponential tilting, and conditional Monte Carlo. Part II contains the new results. We give a series representation of the Pólya-Gamma density valid at every shape parameter b > 0, as an alternating series of first passage densities, and prove the domination inequality that makes its leading term a rejection envelope; the proof combines a union bound over Brownian barriers at b = 1 with the observation that domination is additive along a convolution semigroup. The resulting generator is exact and of constant cost for all b > 0 and c ≥ 0, with acceptance never below 0.84 for b ≤ 1 and 0.67 above it, replacing the saddlepoint approximation that was standard for large b. We give an exact uniformly efficient sampler for the horseshoe local scale, whose conditional we show reduces to the density proportional to e-aη /(1 + η), with acceptance never below 0.6853. We compute the exact acceptance of the r-generalized ratio of uniforms for a Gaussian target in d dimensions, prove that r ⋆ = 1/2 in every dimension, and show the decay is d-d/2 , so the method is intrinsically low-dimensional. We give the expected flip count of the two-coin Bernoulli factory, and a variance study showing that the apparent inefficiency of unbiased MCMC is a tuning artefact: with the burn-in index scaled to the relaxation time the cost-adjusted penalty is between two and eighteen percent for autocorrelations up to 0.99. All numerical claims are verified by simulation or by high-precision quadrature, and the code is supplied.

title: Do Personal AI Conversations Reduce Loneliness? Evidence from a Pre-Registered Experiment
affiliations: , Paris School of Economics (PSE) and Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: Do Personal AI Conversations Reduce Loneliness? Evidence from a Pre-Registered Experiment
detail.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly promoted as a remedy for loneliness. We test this claim in a large-scale pre-registered experiment on a large sample of French adults. Participants assigned to treatment were asked to hold at least one personal conversation a day with a generative AI tool of their choice for 28 days; the control group continued as usual. The intervention raised socio-emotional AI use substantially. This led to an increase in subjective loneliness, a decline in life satisfaction, and a rise in depressive affect and in objective isolation, with more dinners taken alone. The effects are consistently adverse across outcome categories.

title: Efficient Prices, Inefficient Spreads: Attention and Liquidity in Prediction Markets
affiliations: Bentley University - Department of Finance, Bentley University - Department of Finance and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Efficient Prices, Inefficient Spreads: Attention and Liquidity in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: We study how public attention affects bid-ask spreads in prediction markets-a setting where the informed-trader composition channel of attention is identifiable. Using three attention measures constructed entirely outside the order book (Google search interest, Wikipedia pageviews, and news volume) across 232 Kalshi contract series and 667,882 market-day observations over five years, we find that rising attention widens spreads by approximately 3% per standard deviation, reversing the sign of the canonical equity finding. The effect is stronger in complex contracts, concentrates in the announcement hour of FOMC meetings where prices have already converged, and operates through ex-ante defensive quote-setting: makers widen both sides before directional flow arrives, consistent with belief-based pricing of informed-arrival risk rather than reaction to realized order imbalance. An out of-sample test on 2026 World Cup contracts across two venues shows the widening replicates at full strength in thin books and vanishes where depth pins spreads to the tick floor. Prediction-market prices are most expensive to trade on precisely when their informational value peaks-an attention-liquidity paradox that attenuates with institutional depth but persists in sign.

title: Kingman Meets the Horseshoe
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Kingman Meets the Horseshoe
detail.abstract: Kingman's random discrete distributions, completely random measures and partition structures form the probabilistic substrate of Bayesian nonparametrics. We travel in the opposite direction and ask what three strands of modern Bayesian methodology give back to Kingman. The shrinkage weight of the horseshoe prior is exactly the first size-biased frequency of a two-parameter Poisson-Dirichlet law, and the entire Be(a, b) family of shrinkage profiles maps bijectively onto PD(α, θ) through α = 1-a and θ = a + b-1; the horseshoe sits at α = 1/2, which pins its implied sparsity at √ p active coordinates. Separately, the Pólya-Gamma variable is the value of a subordinator in Kingman's sense, and a Jacobi modular transformation of its Lévy density shows it to be an exponentially tempered 1/2-stable subordinator with Blumenthal-Getoor index 1/2. Shrinkage and augmentation therefore turn out to be governed by subordinators of the same index, a coincidence invisible from either construction's own derivation and immediate from Kingman's. On the computational side, Kingman's sufficiency reduction for the Ewens sampling formula turns generative Bayesian computation into a two-dimensional conditional quantile problem; a deep quantile network attains credible-interval coverage matching nominal level to Monte Carlo error at n = 500, while simulation-based calibration with 2 × 10 4 replicates still detects residual miscalibration, and we report both. Finally we prove a moderate deviation principle for the Ewens e-value at speed log n, showing Ville's inequality is tight to exponential order but loose by an Occam factor we compute exactly, and we show that in the two-parameter model evidence about the concentration parameter stops accumulating altogether, so no analogous result exists. Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem supplies almost sure growth rates for maximum-likelihood e-processes under stationary ergodic dependence. Limitations are stated throughout.

title:
Density of Disagreement
Marginal Types in Coordination, Collateral, and Bluffing
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title:
Density of Disagreement
Marginal Types in Coordination, Collateral, and Bluffing
detail.abstract: Disagreement is the state variable. Where it sits sets prices, how dense it is sets fragility, and whether it is public or private decides whether it produces runs or bluffs. On that principle four theories become one: Morris and Shin on global games, Geanakoplos on collateral and the leverage cycle, Borel, von Neumann and Ferguson on poker, and Schelling on manipulated risk. In each, equilibrium is a cutoff fixed by the indifference of a single marginal type, so what matters is not average opinion but opinion at the margin, and not its level but its density. Theorem A splits the response to news into a strategic multiplier 1/(1-ρ) and a quantile term 1/f (t *), so fragility is thin disagreement; since zero-sum games have ρ ≤ 0, poker has no crises and coordination games have nothing else. Theorem B : with common CRRA γ the market belief is the power mean of order 1/γ, so linear opinion pooling is log utility, logarithmic pooling is extreme risk aversion, and the supremum is risk neutrality; collateral truncates that supremum to a quantile whose level is the margin requirement, which is Geanakoplos's marginal buyer. Proposition C reads the favorite-longshot bias as the curvature of that operator, vanishing at γ = 1. Brown and Lin's pari-mutuel fixed point F (P *) = P * is the same equation at full margin, and their supermartingale yields learnability exactly when ρ < 1. Section 11 solves five open problems, among them composite fragility 1/(f h-Cf x), persuasion of a market as persuasion of its marginal buyer, and poker with heterogeneous priors, where all disagreement collapses into one distortion ψ = H • G-1 .

title: The Optimist's Loan: Disagreement Models and the Allocation of Credit
affiliations: University of Padua - Department of Economics and Management , , University at Buffalo (SUNY) - School of Management,  and

detail.title: The Optimist's Loan: Disagreement Models and the Allocation of Credit
detail.abstract: Banks lending to the same firm routinely assign it different default probabilities. Using the euro-area credit register, which records the working risk assessment each bank assigns its borrowers and acts on, we show this disagreement is itself a determinant of credit allocation. Because lending is decentralized, a skeptical bank can cut its exposure but cannot restrict the borrower's aggregate credit, so marginal credit can shift toward the lender holding the most favorable assessment. Instrumented with lenders' housewide rating revisions, disagreement tilts credit toward the most-optimistic lender, who charges less, and predicts bad debt beyond the consensus; the reallocation survives monetary tightening and is not detected in the much smaller syndicated subsample, where lenders operate under a common contract. Credit is allocated at the optimistic margin-an outcome disagreement models obtain from short-sale constraints, and one that arises here from market architecture alone.

title: Learning to Coalesce
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Learning to Coalesce
detail.abstract:
Kingman’s coalescent is the historical home of likelihood-free inference: simulation is trivial and
likelihood evaluation is not. We study generative Bayesian computation for it, and the story
is governed by a sufficiency reduction that exists for Kingman’s exchangeable partitions and
fails here. We first give an exact law that appears not to have been stated in this form: under
the infinite sites model the number of segregating sites is a sum of independent geometrics,
S = Pn
k=2 Sk with Sk ∼ Geom{(k − 1)/(k − 1 + θ)}. This yields Watterson’s mean and
variance in one line, gives an exactly computable likelihood for S, and couples the coalescent to
the Ewens sampling formula: on a common probability space the Ewens block count satisfies
Kn = 1 + #{k : Sk ≥ 1}, so the partition records which coalescent levels carry a mutation
and the site count records how many. Both carry Fisher information θ−1 log n to leading order.
We then show that S is not sufficient for θ, unlike the Ewens block count, so the summary
statistic must be learned rather than derived. We prove a ceiling on what can be learned: any
DeepSets encoder built from per-site permutation-invariant features factors exactly through
the site frequency spectrum, which is a strict coarsening of the maximal invariant, so no such
architecture recovers linkage information at any depth. The number of distinct haplotypes
is a minimal witness that escapes the ceiling, and appending it strictly improves inference.
Experiments confirm the theory. At n = 30 a quantile network matches the exact posterior
given S; the spectrum strictly improves on S, cutting the 90% interval for θ from 85.1 to 61.3 at
constant population size, and under exponential growth removing 33% of the prior width for the
growth rate against 13% for S alone; the haplotype count then improves on the spectrum by a
further 8% while simultaneously improving coverage, but only when it is unsaturated. Because
the likelihood of S under any demography is a one-dimensional integral against the tree-length
law, we can build an exact reference posterior for the growth model and show the learned map
recovers it to within 1.4% on both parameters. Simulation-based calibration nonetheless rejects
exact uniformity throughout; we attempt the standard recalibration repair, show that it fails,
and diagnose the residual error as conditional rather than marginal

title: Measuring the RudriQ Linker: Accuracy, Calibration, and a Trust Envelope for Cross-Domain Data→LLM Provenance

detail.title: Measuring the RudriQ Linker: Accuracy, Calibration, and a Trust Envelope for Cross-Domain Data→LLM Provenance
detail.abstract: Modern ML systems increasingly cross a domain boundary that existing observability tools do not: data prepared by pandas/Spark flows into LLM calls (embeddings, chat completions). The RudriQ linker attempts to recover this data→LLM lineage automatically, attaching a confidence-scored provenance edge from an upstream data artifact to each LLM call. The central question for an audit tool is not whether such a linker exists but whether its links are correct, and that has gone unmeasured, because cross-domain ground truth is hard to establish. We contribute a construction-based benchmark that makes ground truth tractable: pipelines in which we assign every node identity, so the true data→LLM edge set is known by construction, paired with an adversarial arm built to make the linker fail. All findings below are established on this synthetic and adversarial corpus; ecological validation on real third-party pipelines is in progress, and we mark throughout which quantities are portable linker properties and which are corpus-composition-dependent. On the constructed corpus we find: (1) the linker's per-link confidence scale is calibrated in structure: measured precision falls monotonically as stated confidence falls, a structural property (as distinct from the specific per-band precision values, which are composition-dependent); this is the keystone result. (2) the exact-match strategy (object-identity) is near-perfectly precise (precision 1.000, 95% CI [0.987, 1.000], n = 300), and no false positives were observed on representative new data (0 of 200; 95% CI upper bound below 2%). (3) the false-positive surface comprises two bounded, characterized mechanisms that respect their boundaries, yielding a confidence-threshold deployment guideline. (4) common-path instrumentation overhead is below 0.1% of a single LLM call, with two characterized and mitigable fallback costs. This is Paper 2 of the RudriQ/AutoLineage line. AutoLineage (Paper 1) [13] contributes the import-time capture mechanism; this paper measures the cross-domain linker's accuracy and calibration. Same system, different contribution. * Full legal name: Kishan Raj Vandhavasi Goutham Kumar. The author publishes as "Kishan Raj VG.

title: Kakeya in the Transformer: Fibered Complexity of LLM Representations
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Kakeya in the Transformer: Fibered Complexity of LLM Representations
detail.abstract: A large language model approximates an abstract multinomial transition matrix with roughly 10 38,000 rows using roughly 10 12 bits of parameters. That ratio is the entire subject of this paper. Trained transformers organise their last-layer value representations along a single axis aligned with predictive entropy, collapse onto low-dimensional manifolds under domain restriction, and-puzzlingly-lose little Bayesian competence when that axis is ablated. We show these are consequences of a directional compression principle for algorithmic complexity under regular identifiable fibering [Polson and Zantedeschi, 2026]. Reading domain collapse as a fibering and the entropy axis as an along-fiber coordinate, the chain rule for precision-bounded complexity gives K r (v) = K r (d)+K r (v | d)+O(log r), whence the ablation asymmetry: the axis is a sufficient statistic for predictive entropy, not for the fiber label. En route we record that the global convexity hypothesis used to derive continuity of the embedding-to-simplex map [Misra and Dalal, 2024] forces that map to be constant, and repair it locally, reducing the bi-Lipschitz requirement to a spectral condition on the embedding Gram matrix. The principle's two exception clauses-degenerate and adaptively chosen fibering-are shown to be model collapse and in-context learning: the first by a strong data-processing argument, the second by an adaptive-dividend bound whose finite-sample rate is the Beta-Binomial posterior of Misra and Dalal [2024]. We give a computable worked example, relate the Dirichlet-mixture predictive to the universal mixture, read the entropy axis as a linear estimator of instantaneous code length, and propose four experiments, one of them discriminating.

title: Gates are Bayes: Neural Architectures as Approximate Nonlinear Filters
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Gates are Bayes: Neural Architectures as Approximate Nonlinear Filters
detail.abstract: We show that two of the most widely used recursive architectures-the long short-term memory (LSTM) network and the ARCH/GARCH volatility model-are special cases of a single object: the approximate nonlinear filter obtained by applying an assumed-density collapse to the exact Bayes filtering recursion. The organising device is the score-function filter of West [1982] and Masreliez [1975], in which the posterior mean is the prior mean plus a linear transformation of the marginal score of the one-step predictive, m t = a t + P t h t g(u t), with the posterior variance deflated by the corresponding information. Four identities carry the argument. First, the Kalman gain is a logistic sigmoid of the log signal-to-noise ratio, K t = σ(log R t-log V t); this is the LSTM/GRU gate, and it explains why the GRU ties f t = 1-i t. Second, when the observation error is logistic the Bayes score is exactly g(u) = tanh(u/2), and its scale-mixture multiplier ψ(u) = g(u)/u is the Pólya-Gamma conditional mean E[λ | u] with λ | u ∼ PG(2, u) [Polson et al., 2013]: a gate is an imputed latent variable. Third, West's recursions in cell-state coordinates admit exactly two gated representations, a convex one that is the GRU exactly and an innovation one whose candidate is the score; an LSTM combines the forget gate of the first with the candidate of the second, which we show no coherent filter does, so the LSTM is a strict one-parameter-per-unit enlargement of the Bayes filter. Fourth, a discount-Gamma collapse of a stochastic volatility model yields σ2 t = ω + β σ2 t-1 + αy 2 t , and its general non-conjugate form is West's scale score recursion, which is the score-driven (GAS/DCS) update discovered three decades later. We isolate the three approximations-Gaussian collapse, score plug-in, and certainty equivalence-and show numerically that the third alone discards roughly 16% of the exact filtered variance on average and 24% following large innovations, whereas restoring West's variance-of-the-gain term recovers the exact filter to within 0.2%. We close by connecting the exact recursion to generative Bayesian computation [Polson and Sokolov, 2026], in which the posterior map, rather than the filter, is learned.

title: Bayesian Simulation for Stochastic Programs with Chance Constraints
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Washington University

detail.title: Bayesian Simulation for Stochastic Programs with Chance Constraints
detail.abstract: We give a Markov chain Monte Carlo method for stochastic programs with probabilistic (chance) constraints, and organise it around a single principle. Augmenting the decision space by N scenario draws weighted by a symmetric function of an empirical sum yields, on marginalisation, a Boltzmann density penalised either by the cumulant generating function of the augmenting statistic or by its Legendre transform, according to whether the weight is an exponential tilt or a level-set indicator. The chance constraint is the second case applied to the feasibility indicator, giving a Kullback-Leibler penalty between the required and the achieved reliability; an expected-value objective, including two-stage recourse, is the first case, giving an entropic certainty equivalent. The two devices are conjugate, and the same second cumulant governs both of their biases. Reading the marginal as a Boltzmann density identifies the replicate count divided by the temperature as the annealed Lagrange multiplier of the constrained simulated annealing scheme of Geman et al. [1990], and an elementary exact-penalty lemma then supplies everything else. Because the Kullback-Leibler penalty is quadratic rather than linear at the boundary, it is never exact: a linear cooling schedule K t ≳ rκ t suffices for δ-optimality with r > L 2 /2δ in terms of the calmness modulus L, but the chain equilibrates at a reliability short of nominal by α(1-α)ν/r, where ν is the shadow price of reliability. We give the exact stationarity equation, its first-order solution, and a threshold tightening that removes the shortfall using only two pilot chains to estimate ν. The parallel result for the objective block is a risk-seeking tilt of order κ/2J, which sharpens the replicate device of Ekin et al. [2014, 2017]. The method requires no convexity, no deterministic equivalent, no binarisation of the distribution and no mixed integer reformulation, and handles joint chance constraints with no modification. It returns the entire near-optimal set rather than a single point. We validate against an exactly solvable Gaussian chance-constrained programme, where the bias formulas are confirmed without fitted parameters, and then solve a pension asset-liability problem with a joint chance constraint on interim and terminal funding, heavy-tailed returns and piecewise linear recourse.

title: What Does a Million Dollars Buy You? Measuring the Relative Value of Wealth Across Time
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: What Does a Million Dollars Buy You? Measuring the Relative Value of Wealth Across Time
detail.abstract: During much of the twentieth century, accumulating one million dollars represented the canonical milestone of economic success in the United States. Standard practice adjusts historical monetary quantities for consumer price inflation, suggesting that one million dollars in 1950 is equivalent to approximately thirteen million dollars today. We argue that this approach, while appropriate for measuring purchasing power, fails to capture what made the million-dollar threshold economically and socially significant. We develop a unified framework in which all equivalence measures arise as special cases of a single intertemporal welfare problem parameterized by the weight placed on absolute consumption versus relative social position. We propose and compare five equivalence measures grounded in distinct notions of what wealth fundamentally represents: purchasing power, command over labor, relative social status, economic influence as a share of GDP, and share of aggregate private wealth. Applying these measures to U.S. data from 1950 to 2024, we show that the equivalences diverge substantially and increasingly after 1980, with the modern equivalent of one million dollars in 1950 ranging from approximately $13 million under CPI adjustment to $170 million under the status-preserving measure. Under a synthetic equal-weights index, the modern equivalent is approximately $92 million. We further examine whether a 1950 millionaire could have preserved their relative status through investment in Treasury bills, government bonds, equities, or real estate, finding a striking asymmetry: only equity investors consistently kept pace with the threshold required to maintain relative social standing, with one million dollars invested in the S&P 500 in 1950 growing to approximately two billion dollars by 2024. Our results suggest that the Consumer Price Index systematically understates the cost of occupying a given position in the economic hierarchy, with direct implications for the design of inflation-indexed fiscal thresholds.

title: Generative Bayesian Computation for Volatility Surfaces
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, George Mason University and

detail.title: Generative Bayesian Computation for Volatility Surfaces
detail.abstract: We develop Generative Bayesian Computation (GBC) for implied volatility surfaces. The surface is a spatial random field on a degenerate, rolling design of traded strikes and expiries. We model it as a structural stochastic volatility component plus a sparse spatial discrepancy field carrying a horseshoe prior, and we infer both by training a deep quantile network on forward simulations to learn the inverse Bayes map. Inference is amortized: the posterior for a new surface is one forward pass, so rough volatility models with no closed-form prices become estimable across millions of surface-days. Two constructions make the posterior trustworthy. No-arbitrage is imposed by architecture-a monotone mixture-of-Black parameterization-so butterfly, calendar and bound constraints hold exactly at every draw. The inverse map is learned in triangular form, which delivers the joint posterior rather than its marginals; this matters because we measure a Jacobian correlation of 0.97 between volatility-of-volatility and leverage, a ridge that a coordinatewise construction would report as independent uncertainty. Applied to thirty years of S&P 500 and single-name options, GBC lowers out-of-sample surface error relative to dynamic semiparametric factor models and arbitrage-free SVI, with gains concentrated in the short-tenor wings. A delta-vega hedged strategy earns a Sharpe ratio monotone in posterior certainty-a ranking point-estimate methods cannot form.

title: Beyond Chernoff-Stein: Moderate Deviations and Bayes Testing
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Beyond Chernoff-Stein: Moderate Deviations and Bayes Testing
detail.abstract: We revisit the informationtheoretic treatment of hypothesis testing in Chapter 11 of Cover and Thomas (2006) and extend it in three directions. First, we recast the ChernoStein lemma and Cherno information as consequences of Sanov's theorem on the simplex of types, which makes the extension to omposite nulls and alternatives immediate: the error exponent becomes an inmum of KullbackLeibler divergence over an I-projection, and Hoeding's generalised likelihood-ratio test attains it universally. Second, we replace the large-deviation scale by the moderteEdevition scale λ n ≍ (log n)/n. On this scale the divergence functional linearises to its Hessian, a χ 2 quadratic form; the Stein exponent collapses, error probabilities decay polynomilly rather than exponentially, and the BahadurRao prefactor becomes the leading source of information. Third, following Datta et al. (2026a), we show that integrated Bayes risk for a composite alternative selects precisely this moderate-deviation boundary, producing a threshold t 2 crit = log n + log(c-2 π)-log(2πσ 2) + 2 log(π 0 /π a) + o(1), i.e. the ChernoStein exponent-nD augmented by a 1 2 log n (EfronTruax), a d 2 log n (RubinSethuraman/BIC) and an O(1) prior-dependent term. A worked political polling example quanties the dierences: to separate a 5248 race from a dead heat one needs n ≈ 5,800 under a Stein criterion but n ≈ 23,000 under a symmetric Bayes criterion, and a poll of n = 1,000 showing 53.1% is signicant at 5% while the Bayes factor favours the dead heat by 5.8 : 1.

title: Borrowing After the Storm: Hurricanes and the Cost of Municipal Debt
affiliations: Liaoning University and Tulane University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Borrowing After the Storm: Hurricanes and the Cost of Municipal Debt
detail.abstract: Natural disasters can tighten public finance when recovery needs rise. We link U.S. municipal bond offerings from 2000 to 2019 to county hurricane exposure and estimate a stacked difference-indifferences design within a common population with realized hurricane exposure. Severe exposure raises new issue borrowing costs by approximately 7-30 bps across reported estimands and reduces issuance probability, bond counts, and par amounts. The contraction extends to non-refunding infrastructure debt. Repricing peaks during the first six months, is larger where realized losses are greater, and dissipates within two years. FEMA project histories show that much emergency support remains administratively unresolved early in recovery. The response does not increase with maturity, and outstanding bonds exhibit no comparable repricing. The evidence points to a temporary primary market tightening concentrated in new public debt.

title: Verification Before Payment and Reported Loss in Tanzanian Diaspora Real Estate Transactions: Exploratory Evidence from Mainland Tanzania

detail.title: Verification Before Payment and Reported Loss in Tanzanian Diaspora Real Estate Transactions: Exploratory Evidence from Mainland Tanzania

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Founder and Managing Principal of Terranova APRIL US LLC (United States) and Terranova Company Limited (Tanzania), property and investment-advisory firms whose work may involve transaction-verification practices discussed in this paper. This interest is disclosed because it may be relevant to the interpretation of the pilot evidence and proposed future research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This exploratory survey was conducted independently outside an institutional ethics-review system; no formal ethics approval or exemption determination was obtained. Participation was voluntary and respondents provided informed consent before proceeding. No personally identifying transaction details are reported.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This exploratory pilot study examines transaction controls and self-reported monetary loss among Tanzanians abroad who reported a completed or attempted real-estate transaction in mainland Tanzania. An open online questionnaire circulated through diaspora networks from 7 to 13 July 2026. Twenty eligible adult responses were analysed, including 13 respondents with a completed or attempted mainland property transaction. Five of the 12 transactors who answered the loss question reported losing money beyond ordinary transaction costs, and 8 of 13 reported that they had not obtained an independent valuation. Among respondents with complete data, none of the four who reported an independent title or right-holder check before payment reported a loss, compared with five of eight who did not report such a check before payment. The sample is small, self-selected, non-random, open-link and not preregistered, so this difference is descriptive rather than confirmatory. The same direction appeared when the analysis was limited to completed transactions (0 of 3 verified versus 5 of 7 not verified), although the numbers were too small for reliable inference. A purposive review of documentary sources places the survey measures in the mainland Tanzanian context, where competing land allocations, fraudulent title issuance, construction-fund diversion, uncertain boundaries and costly dispute resolution have all been documented. The findings do not establish population prevalence or a causal effect. They provide pilot evidence on measurable transaction exposures and inform the design of a future preregistered study of verification before non-refundable payment.

title: The Exact Dimensional Threshold for Spearman Rank-Correlation Compatibility
affiliations: University of Waterloo - Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science and Stanford University

detail.title: The Exact Dimensional Threshold for Spearman Rank-Correlation Compatibility
detail.abstract: We show that, for a given dimension, the set of Spearman's rank correlation matrices and that of linear correlation matrices coincide if and only if the dimension is no larger than nine. For this, we construct an extreme rank-four counterexample in dimension ten and prove its incompatibility using moment identities and Cauchy-Schwarz. Appending unit directions produces counterexamples in every higher dimension. This, together with existing results, completes the dimensional classification and settles a long-standing open question in quantitative risk management.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of modern portfolio management methodologies, bridging the gap between classical foundational frameworks and cutting-edge computational intelligence. We begin by reviewing traditional asset allocation models, specifically the Markowitz Mean-Variance optimization framework, to anchor the core mathematical trade-offs between risk and expected return. Recognizing the practical limitations of classical frameworks-such as extreme sensitivity to input parameters and estimation errors-we systematically explore advanced allocation techniques. These include the Black-Litterman model, probabilistic scenario optimization, prospect theory, the Kelly criterion, and risk parity frameworks across diverse asset classes. Beyond traditional extensions, this research integrates advanced econometrics and machine learning algorithms to enhance predictive accuracy and portfolio robustness. We investigate the application of deep neural networks for asset return forecasting, genetic algorithms for heuristic constraint optimization, information theory for feature selection, and reinforcement learning for dynamic, multi-period policy execution. Through rigorous mathematical formalization and robust Python implementations, this paper demonstrates how combining statistical machine learning with behavioral and probabilistic asset allocation paradigms yields superior risk-adjusted performance in highly volatile market regimes.

title: Bounding the Value of China's Pet Medical Insurance: Evidence from Six Reimbursement Contracts

detail.title: Bounding the Value of China's Pet Medical Insurance: Evidence from Six Reimbursement Contracts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study uses publicly available contract terms and aggregate secondary information and does not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, or animal experimentation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: China's pet medical insurance market has expanded rapidly, yet prospective buyers lack the information needed to compare policies, and the claims microdata required for welfare or lossratio analysis are not public. This paper evaluates six reimbursement contracts sold by China Continent Insurance (Dadi) and ZhongAn Online, drawing on their contract terms together with two publicly reported statistics-a claim-frequency band and a single average-cost figure drawn from corporate disclosures carried in the financial press. Payout functions are reconstructed from the policy documents and validated against published claims examples. The two statistics fix claim frequency and average claim size but leave the claim-size distribution unidentified, so welfare cannot be point-identified. The paper instead derives bounds holding over every claimsize distribution consistent with the anchored mean: on expected annual indemnity, on the incremental indemnity from a tier upgrade, and, under a stated limit on severity support, on the certainty equivalent. Conditional on either labeled reading of the cost anchor, five of the six contracts have money's-worth upper bounds of 21-42 percent of premium, and an additional yuan of premium spent on a tier upgrade returns at most RMB 0.50 in expected indemnity. Pervisit caps and reimbursement rates, rather than the annual limits emphasized in marketing, govern attainable payouts. It is a contract-level case study of six policies on a single platform and develops a method for term-based comparison when contracts are public but claims files are not; it is not a market-wide welfare assessment.

detail.abstract: General-purpose large language models (LLMs) increasingly influence how people seek medical care, yet medical knowledge alone does not guarantee safe triage. We distinguish two complementary dimensions for evaluating public-facing LLMs: Informational Influence and Clinical Authority (IF/CA). Drawing on legal and regulatory examples from China and the United States, together with a stakeholder survey, we show that governance responsibilities can arise before a system ever acquires formal clinical authority. We argue that governance should instead track a system's influence on healthcare utilization and its capacity to prevent harm.

title: Where to Spend a Memory Budget in Gauss-Newton Preconditioning?
affiliations: ,  Universitas Islam Darul, Universitas Islam Negeri Maulana Malik Ibrahim, Malang, Universitas Islam Negeri Maulana Malik Ibrahim, Malang, Universitas Islam Negeri Maulana Malik Ibrahim, Malang, Universitas Islam Negeri Maulana Malik Ibrahim, Malang, Universitas Islam Negeri Maulana Malik Ibrahim Malang, Students, Universitas Islam Negeri Maulana Malik Ibrahim Malang, Students and Universitas Islam Negeri Maulana Malik Ibrahim, Malang

detail.title: Where to Spend a Memory Budget in Gauss-Newton Preconditioning?
detail.abstract: Block-diagonal generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) methods cut the cost of second-order optimization, but their blocks are fixed by architecture or by a manual block size. We show that this fixing hides a computational obstruction: selecting the partition that minimizes the discarded curvature residual under a quadratic memory budget is NP-hard in the strong sense, and stays NP-hard even without a budget once blocks are capped at three parameters. We therefore select the blocks from the observed curvature under a global quadratic memory budget, ranking candidate merges by discarded-residual gain per unit of storage, agglomerating them into a hierarchy, and allocating the budget exactly over its tree cuts. The selection carries guarantees on both sides. A priori, we prove an exact merge-residual identity, descent, line-search convergence uniform over the selected partitions, and an explicit bound on the deviation from the full damped-GGN step. A posteriori, a fractional pair-packing relaxation lower-bounds the residual of every admissible partition, so each selected partition ships with a computable certificate of its optimality gap; at the scarcest ceilings the certificate is exact on the real-data snapshot, within 35% on the controlled diagnostic, and complete enumeration confirms both. Across ten-seed experiments on shallow and two-hidden-layer networks the selected partition attains the lowest discarded residual and the lowest realized step error at every matched ceiling, with 23-47% of its retained coupling crossing layer boundaries, where architecture-aligned baselines retain none. A sweep of 390 damping configurations sharpens the regime claim into a dose-response law: the residual ordering tracks the realized step whenever the certified factor ∥R P ∥ 2 /λ is at most one, the tracking inverts beyond ten, and a certified pairwise test converts individual comparisons into proofs without any full solve. A matrix-free instantiation carries the selection, with both certificates, to a 38,151-parameter network in which the dense GGN could not be stored, running entirely from a one-megabyte table of atom couplings.

title: Patriarchal Systems and the Reproduction of Gender Inequality in South Asia: A Structural Analysis of Child Marriage, Education, and Social Norms
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Patriarchal Systems and the Reproduction of Gender Inequality in South Asia: A Structural Analysis of Child Marriage, Education, and Social Norms
detail.abstract: Gender inequality in South Asia remains a persistent social issue despite progress in education, legal reforms, and development indicators. This paper investigates how patriarchal systems contribute to the continuation of gender inequality by examining the interconnected roles of child marriage, education, and social norms. The study addresses the gap between formal advancements in gender equality and the continued existence of practices that restrict girls' and women's autonomy. Using a qualitative secondary research methodology, this study analyzes feminist theoretical frameworks, academic literature, and reports from international organizations to explore how family structures, cultural expectations, economic conditions, and institutional practices influence gender relations. Drawing on Sylvia Walby's theory of patriarchy and Kalwant Bhopal's intersectional perspective, the research examines how multiple systems operate together to reproduce unequal opportunities and social expectations. The findings demonstrate that child marriage is sustained through interconnected factors, including family honor systems, gendered expectations surrounding sexuality, economic insecurity, and assumptions regarding women's traditional roles. The analysis further reveals that improvements in educational access alone are insufficient to eliminate gender inequality when broader social, cultural, and economic structures continue to limit female agency. This paper concludes that meaningful progress requires structural transformation rather than isolated interventions. Addressing gender inequality demands changes in the systems and institutions that shape girls' opportunities, rights, and social value. Future research should continue examining how local contexts influence gender relations and how policy approaches can better address the underlying causes of inequality.

title: Effect on Trade between Member States (Articles 101 and 102 TFEU)

detail.title: Effect on Trade between Member States (Articles 101 and 102 TFEU)
detail.abstract: The criterion “effect on trade between Member States” has a central role in determining the application of EU competition rules across the Union. Its conceptualisation serves to distinguish cases covered by EU law from those addressed by national law. The criterion is integral to the application of all competition rules, including merger and State aid provisions. However, this entry explores the interpretation of the criterion in relation to the application of Articles 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (“TFEU”). The analysis focuses on the European Union's interpretation of the effect on trade criterion, examining its application to various agreements and unilateral conduct, and providing some examples of divergent national approaches.

title: Information Design and Entry in Auctions
affiliations: , Università degli Studi di Firenze and Universit`a degli Studi di Firenze

detail.title: Information Design and Entry in Auctions
detail.abstract: This paper is about a two-bidder auction setting with endogenous and costly entry in which, before the bidders' entry decisions, the seller may release information about the object on sale. This information affects each bidder's belief about the own distribution of value for the object on sale, hence it affects the bidder's incentive to enter. The seller uses a second price auction and we consider the class of unrestricted information structures using the techniques of information design in which the seller sends private messages to the bidders. We characterize the optimal information structure, which optimally trades off providing rents to the bidders in favorable (to the bidders) states of the world against inducing entry of all bidders in other states of the world (in order to generate a positive auction revenue). We compare the optimal information structure with some specific information structures examined in the literature and then show that a restriction to public messages hurts the seller significantly. We also show that using a first price auction allows the seller to earn the same revenue as when a second price auction is used. We then allow the seller to use an entry fee and jointly optimize, under some restrictions, with respect to the entry fee and the information structure. In this case the seller does not need to induce entry of all bidders to earn a positive revenue, and indeed induces entry of a single bidder, who is required to pay a high entry fee, if the entry cost is not small. But if the seller can also use a reserve price, then it is optimal to (almost) fully subsidize the entry cost and use the reserve price to extract all the bidders' rents while inducing the socially optimal entry.

title: Granular Networks and the Pricing of Indirect Transition Risk
affiliations: University of Turin - Collegio Carlo Alberto

detail.title: Granular Networks and the Pricing of Indirect Transition Risk

declarations.funderStatement: The author acknowledges financial support under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), Mission 4, Component 2, Investment 1.1, Call for tender No. 1409 published on 14.9.2022 by the Italian Ministry of University and Research (MUR), funded by the European Union – NextGenerationEU – Project Title "Measuring, managing and hedging indirect climate-transition risks" – CUP P20228CHNL - Grant Assignment Decree No. 1376 adopted on 01/09/2023 by the Italian Ministry of Ministry of University and Research (MUR).

detail.abstract: This paper builds a theoretical asset-pricing model to rationalize the sign, magnitude, and cross-sectional pattern of indirect climate-transition-risk pricing documented empirically for European manufacturing firms. Firms source intermediate inputs from many suppliers organized along an input-output network; each supplier's environmental performance combines a sector-wide systematic component with idiosyncratic noise. Aggregating supplier scores within a sector, as in an input-output-weighted portfolio, averages out idiosyncratic noise and recovers a clean, priced systematic factor, whereas measures based on a single bilateral supplier relationship remain dominated by noise and are attenuated toward zero. Combining this granular production-network structure with investors' nonpecuniary demand for green holdings delivers a negative price of indirect-transition risk, consistent with the data. The model further predicts that larger, better-diversified firms load more heavily on the systemic factor, rationalizing its observed correlation with size. Calibrated simulations reproduce the empirical magnitudes of both the risk premium and the bilateral attenuation. Beyond its asset-pricing implications, the model bears directly on climate-transition-risk disclosure policy: supply-chain risk metrics built on a handful of tracked bilateral relationships, as favoured by several current disclosure frameworks, are shown to be statistically uninformative even when the underlying network exposure is large and priced, whereas sector-level, input-output-weighted aggregation recovers that exposure with far greater precision, using data on input-output linkages and supplier emissions that regulators and standard-setters already collect.

detail.title:
The Impact of Financial Liberalization Policy on the Development of Financial Sectors in Ethiopia- An ARDL Modeling
Approaches
detail.abstract:
The study analyzes the impact of financial liberalization policy on the development of the
financial sector in Ethiopia during the period 1973-2005. Specifically, it investigates whether
financial liberalization policy exerts a different effect on the financial sectors development in the
short run and long run, whether; there are differences in various financial reform policies. To that
end the paper employs persaran’s (2001) bound test to the ARDL model. The sources of the data
are World Bank, International Monterey Fund, National Bank of Ethiopia and Ministry of
Finance and Economic Development of Ethiopia. The finding of the study shows that in the long
run financial liberalization policy has positive and statistically significant impact on the
development of financial sectors. But in the short run it didn’t have any impacts on the
development of financial sectors. Liberalization in banking supervision is the most effective and
efficient financial liberalization policy in Ethiopia. The positive impacts of the financial
liberalization policy show the better implementation status of the Ethiopia governments. The
policy implication of the study is that the Ethiopia government should have to fasten the full
liberalization of financial sectors to maximize the benefit for the country

title: Factors Influencing the Performance of World Bank-Funded Projects: Evidence from Woliso Town, Ethiopia
affiliations: and Oromia State University

detail.title: Factors Influencing the Performance of World Bank-Funded Projects: Evidence from Woliso Town, Ethiopia

publicationDetails.detailsText: KDI School of Pub Policy & Management Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: KDI School of Public Policy & Management Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examined the factors affecting the performance of World Bank-funded projects in Woliso Town. The study focused on assessing the influence of stakeholder involvement, staff competencies, monitoring and evaluation, and resource availability on the performance of World Bank-funded projects. A descriptive and explanatory research design was employed using a quantitative research approach. Data were collected from 296 respondents through self-administered questionnaires, and the collected data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression analysis with the support of SPSS. The findings revealed that stakeholder involvement, staff competencies, monitoring and evaluation, and resource availability had a significant positive effect on the performance of World Bank-funded projects. The correlation analysis indicated a significant positive relationship between all independent variables and project performance. Furthermore, the regression model showed that the selected factors explained 67.5% of the variation in project performance. Among the factors, resource availability was found to be the strongest predictor of project performance, followed by staff competencies, monitoring and evaluation, and stakeholder 2 involvement. The study concluded that successful implementation of World Bank-funded projects requires effective stakeholder engagement, competent project personnel, continuous monitoring and evaluation, and adequate availability and utilization of resources. Therefore, the study recommends strengthening stakeholder participation, improving staff capacity through continuous training, institutionalizing monitoring and evaluation practices, and enhancing resource mobilization and management to improve the effectiveness and sustainability of World Bank-funded projects in Woliso Town.

title:
Reframing Systemic Fragility as a Latent Structural Condition:
 A Conceptual Framework for Financial Stability Analysis

detail.title:
Reframing Systemic Fragility as a Latent Structural Condition:
 A Conceptual Framework for Financial Stability Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper involving no human or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Conventional financial stability monitoring treats systemic risk as something observable, composite stress indices built from volatility, credit spreads, and liquidity signals. These indices have repeatedly registered calm in the periods immediately preceding major crises. This paper argues the failure is conceptual rather than methodological: the object of measurement has been misidentified.Systemic fragility is not an event to be predicted. It is a latent structural condition to be detected, one that accumulates within the financial system well before it becomes visible in any market indicator. Three features distinguish it from observable stress: latency, structural persistence, and regime dependence. The paper identifies four structural dimensions through which latent fragility expresses itself, risk concentration, risk persistence, market functioning, and shock transmission, and argues that only the joint activation of all four constitutes a fragile regime. Any lesser configuration is a known type of market disturbance, not a systemic condition.Central to the framework is the structural-observability gap: the interval by which structural-regime transitions precede observable stress in conventional indicators. If that gap is real and measurable, it is also the window in which preventive intervention is possible. Three testable propositions are advanced. Empirical operationalization; including construction of the Latent Fragility Index, is developed in companion work.
